The oblique force turns the door less strongly because its lever arm is 64 cm, shorter than 80 cm. For a force acting along the door toward the hinge, the line of action passes through \(O\), the lever arm is zero, and so is the moment.

2.8.3 The second condition of equilibrium

Now we can write as an equation what it means that the forces do not tend to turn a body. Let forces \(\vek F_1, \vek F_2, \dots, \vek F_{\mathrm{k}}\) act on a body at points \(A_1, A_2, \dots, A_{\mathrm{k}}\), and let \(O\) be a chosen point. The forces do not tend to turn the body when the sum of their moments about \(O\) is the zero vector:

\[\vek r_1\times\vek F_1 + \vek r_2\times\vek F_2 + \dots + \vek r_{\mathrm{k}}\times\vek F_{\mathrm{k}} = \vek 0 , \tag{2.35}\]

where \(\vek r_1 = \overrightarrow{OA_1}\) is the vector from \(O\) to the point at which the force \(\vek F_1\) acts, and the same for the other forces. This is the second condition of equilibrium of definition 2.3, written with numbers (SADD §3.7, (3.7.6), PDF pp. 77-78, EP §2.2.2, p. 54). When a force is distributed over a part of the surface or over all the material, like the weight, it is by section 2.1 the sum of many small forces, one on each bit, and its moment is the sum of their moments. Equation (2.35) is a vector equation, so it means three equations for numbers, one for each component.

Where does this condition come from? Like the condition for the forces, it is a law of mechanics that we do not derive from others. CM writes it for every part of a body, also for a body that moves: the sum of the moments of all forces on a part of a body equals the rate at which the sum of the moments of the momenta (gibalne količine) of its bits changes, the momentum of a bit being its mass times its velocity. CM calls it the principle of balance of angular momentum (načelo o vrtilni količini) (CM §5.3.3, (5.3.28), PDF pp. 232-233). For a body at rest all velocities are zero, the right side is zero, and (2.35) remains. We cannot get it from the condition for the forces, as the ruler shows.

Let the ruler in figure 2.3 be 30 cm long. We put the origin \(O\) at its centre, the axis \(x\) along the ruler, the axis \(y\) horizontally across it and the axis \(z\) vertically up (figure 2.43). The ends are \(A_1 = (15, 0, 0)\) cm and \(A_2 = (-15, 0, 0)\) cm. The force \(\vek F = (0, 5, 0)\) N acts on the right end, the force \(-\vek F\) on the left end. The resultant is zero, and the first condition of equilibrium holds. The moments about \(O\), however, are

\[(15, 0, 0)\times(0, 5, 0) = (0, 0, 75)\ \text{N cm} , \qquad (-15, 0, 0)\times(0, -5, 0) = (0, 0, 75)\ \text{N cm} .\]

Their sum \((0, 0, 150)\) N cm is not the zero vector, and the second condition does not hold. The moment points vertically up. From the tip of the axis \(z\), from above, we see the ruler turn from the axis \(x\) toward the axis \(y\), counterclockwise, as the grey arrow in figure 2.3 shows. The forces along the ruler, \((5, 0, 0)\) N at the right end and \((-5, 0, 0)\) N at the left end, have the moments

\[(15, 0, 0)\times(5, 0, 0) = \vek 0 , \qquad (-15, 0, 0)\times(-5, 0, 0) = \vek 0 ,\]

because the vector to the point of action points in the direction of the force or opposite to it. The line of action therefore passes through \(O\), and the lever arm is zero (lemma 2.33 on the lever arm and the magnitude of the moment). Such forces do not turn the ruler. In section 2.1 we claimed this for bars pulled along their axis, and now it is proved.

About which point \(O\) should we compute the moments? For the ruler, let us choose the left end \(A_2\) instead of the centre. The vector from \(A_2\) to \(A_1\) is \((30, 0, 0)\) cm, and the vector from \(A_2\) to \(A_2\) is the zero vector, so the sum of the moments is

\[(30, 0, 0)\times(0, 5, 0) + \vek 0\times(0, -5, 0) = (0, 0, 150)\ \text{N cm} ,\]

the same as about the centre. This is no coincidence.

Lemma 2.34 The moment does not depend on the point (moment ni odvisen od točke)

Let forces \(\vek F_1, \vek F_2, \dots, \vek F_{\mathrm{k}}\) act at points \(A_1, A_2, \dots, A_{\mathrm{k}}\), and let their resultant be the zero vector, \(\vek F_1 + \vek F_2 + \dots + \vek F_{\mathrm{k}} = \vek 0\). Then for any two points \(O\) and \(Q\)

\[\overrightarrow{QA_1}\times\vek F_1 + \dots + \overrightarrow{QA_{\mathrm{k}}}\times\vek F_{\mathrm{k}} = \overrightarrow{OA_1}\times\vek F_1 + \dots + \overrightarrow{OA_{\mathrm{k}}}\times\vek F_{\mathrm{k}} .\]
Proof

We write each vector from \(Q\) to one of the points \(A_1, \dots, A_{\mathrm{k}}\) as a path through the point \(O\) and use the splitting of a sum.

  1. Let \(\vek d = \overrightarrow{QO}\). By (1.8), \(\overrightarrow{QA_1} = \vek d + \overrightarrow{OA_1}\), since for example \(x_{\mathrm{A}_1} - x_{\mathrm{Q}} = (x_{\mathrm{O}} - x_{\mathrm{Q}}) + (x_{\mathrm{A}_1} - x_{\mathrm{O}})\), and the same for the coordinates \(y\) and \(z\). The same holds for the other points.
  2. By item 2 of lemma 2.31 on the properties of the vector product, \(\overrightarrow{QA_1}\times\vek F_1 = \vek d\times\vek F_1 + \overrightarrow{OA_1}\times\vek F_1\), and the same for the other forces.
  3. We add all \(k\) equalities. The terms with \(\vek d\) give, by the same item 2 applied to the second factor, \(\vek d\times\vek F_1 + \dots + \vek d\times\vek F_{\mathrm{k}} = \vek d\times(\vek F_1 + \dots + \vek F_{\mathrm{k}}) = \vek d\times\vek 0\).
  4. By item 3 of the same lemma, applied with the number zero, \(\vek d\times\vek 0 = \vek d\times(0\,\vek d) = 0\,(\vek d\times\vek d) = \vek 0\). What remains is the sum of the moments about \(O\).

Source: SADD §3.7 (PDF p. 78) says that the point about which the moments are computed can be chosen arbitrarily. The lemma and the proof are not from the sources.

So when the resultant of the forces is zero, the second condition of equilibrium does not depend on the choice of the point \(O\). If the sum of the moments is zero about one point, it is zero about every point. We can therefore choose the point that makes the computation shortest, for example one through which as many lines of action as possible pass, since forces on these lines have no moment. For the ruler the lemma says that the pair of forces \(\vek F\) and \(-\vek F\) turns it with the moment \((0, 0, 150)\) N cm no matter about which point we compute it.

2.8.4 Moments on a small cube

We now apply the second condition of equilibrium to the same small cube to which we applied the first condition in section 2.7. Let the body be in equilibrium and \(P\) a point in its interior. We put the origin of a right-handed rectangular Cartesian coordinate system at \(P\). In thought we cut out of the body the cube with centre \(P\), side \(h\) and edges parallel to the axes. Its faces lie in the planes \(x = \pm h/2\), \(y = \pm h/2\) and \(z = \pm h/2\). The cube is a part of a body in equilibrium, so it is in equilibrium itself (section 2.1), and by (2.35) the sum of the moments of all forces on it about \(P\) is the zero vector. Two kinds of forces act on the cube. The rest of the body acts on it across its six faces, and the body force (definition 2.26), for example the weight, acts on all its material. Its density \(\vek b\) is the force per unit volume.

We know the force across a face from the stress components. As in section 2.7 we write the point with the traction vector, \(\vek t(Q, \vek n)\), because we compare traction vectors at different points. On the face \(x = h/2\) the outward normal of the cube is \(\vek e_{\mathrm{x}}\), and at a point \(Q\) of this face the traction vector \(\vek t(Q, \vek e_{\mathrm{x}}) = \big(\sigma_{\mathrm{xx}}(Q), \sigma_{\mathrm{xy}}(Q), \sigma_{\mathrm{xz}}(Q)\big)\) acts per unit area (definition 2.25). On the opposite face \(x = -h/2\) the outward normal is \(-\vek e_{\mathrm{x}}\), and by lemma 2.21 on the traction on the opposite side of a cut the traction at its point \(Q\) is \(\vek t(Q, -\vek e_{\mathrm{x}}) = -\vek t(Q, \vek e_{\mathrm{x}})\). The same holds on the other four faces. The stress components change from point to point, so the force is not necessarily distributed evenly over a face.

We treat a distributed force as in sections 2.1 and 2.7, as the sum of many small forces on small patches. We divide a face of the cube by lines parallel to its sides into equal small rectangles. On a rectangle with the area \(\Delta A\) and the centre \(Q\) the force \(\vek t(Q)\,\Delta A\) acts at \(Q\), where \(\vek t(Q)\) is the force per unit area at \(Q\), on the face \(x = h/2\) therefore \(\vek t(Q, \vek e_{\mathrm{x}})\). The moment of the distributed force is the sum of the moments of these small forces. In the same way we divide the volume of the cube into equal small cubes. This is a simplification, and in section 2.7 we took the same summation as an assumption about the forces on the faces of the cube. SADD and CM write the moment of a distributed force exactly, by exact adding up over a surface and over a body (SADD (3.7.6), PDF p. 78, CM (5.3.28), PDF p. 233), which we will meet in chapter 4. Until then we compute with sums. We need two facts about them, collected in lemma 2.35.

Lemma 2.35 Moment of a distributed force (moment porazdeljene sile)

Let a force act on a flat face with the area \(A\), equal per unit area to \(\vek t(Q)\) at the point \(Q\). We divide the face into small bits. On a bit with the area \(\Delta A\) the force \(\vek t(Q)\,\Delta A\) acts at a chosen point \(Q\) of the bit, and the moment of the distributed force about a point \(O\) is the sum of the moments of these forces. Then:

  1. If the face is a rectangle with the centre \(S\), divided by lines parallel to its sides into equal rectangles, the points \(Q\) are their centres, and the force is distributed evenly, \(\vek t(Q) = \vek t_0\) for all \(Q\), then its moment about \(O\) equals \(\overrightarrow{OS}\times(A\,\vek t_0)\), the moment of the resultant \(A\,\vek t_0\) acting at the centre \(S\).
  2. If \(|\vek t(Q)| \le c\) for all chosen points \(Q\) and every point of the face is at most \(r_{\max}\) away from \(O\), then every component of the moment is at most \(c\,A\,r_{\max}\) in absolute value.

Item 2 holds in the same way for a force distributed over a volume \(V\), equal per unit volume to \(\vek b(Q)\), with \(|\vek b(Q)| \le c\) at all chosen points \(Q\) of the bits of volume. Every component of its moment is then at most \(c\,V\,r_{\max}\).

Proof

We show both statements on the sum of the moments of the small forces.

1. An evenly distributed force.

  1. Lines parallel to the sides divide each side into equal parts, so the division is the same on both sides of the centre \(S\). A rectangle whose centre is moved from \(S\) by a vector \(\vek s\) has a partner whose centre is moved from \(S\) by \(-\vek s\). When the number of rectangles is odd in both directions, the middle rectangle has its centre at \(S\) and is its own partner.
  2. All rectangles have the same area \(\Delta A\), so the same force \(\vek f = \vek t_0\,\Delta A\) acts on each. The vectors from \(O\) to the centres of a pair are \(\overrightarrow{OS} + \vek s\) and \(\overrightarrow{OS} - \vek s\).
  3. By items 2 and 3 of lemma 2.31 on the properties of the vector product, the sum of the moments of the pair is
    \[(\overrightarrow{OS} + \vek s)\times\vek f + (\overrightarrow{OS} - \vek s)\times\vek f = 2\,\overrightarrow{OS}\times\vek f + \vek s\times\vek f - \vek s\times\vek f = 2\,\overrightarrow{OS}\times\vek f .\]
    The middle rectangle, if there is one, has the moment \(\overrightarrow{OS}\times\vek f\).
  4. Each rectangle therefore contributes \(\overrightarrow{OS}\times\vek f\) to the sum, as if its force acted at \(S\). By item 2 of the same lemma the sum is \(\overrightarrow{OS}\times(\vek f + \vek f + \dots + \vek f)\). The sum of the forces is \(\vek t_0\) times the sum of the areas, that is, \(A\,\vek t_0\).

2. A bound for the moment.

  1. Take one bit of the division with the chosen point \(Q\) and the force \(\vek f = \vek t(Q)\,\Delta A\), and let \(\vek r = \overrightarrow{OQ}\). By item 5 of the lemma on the properties of the vector product, \(|\vek r\times\vek f|^2 = |\vek r|^2\,|\vek f|^2 - (\vek r\cdot\vek f)^2 \le |\vek r|^2\,|\vek f|^2\), so by lemma 1.28 that a larger nonnegative number has a larger square, \(|\vek r\times\vek f| \le |\vek r|\,|\vek f|\).
  2. We have \(|\vek r| \le r_{\max}\), and by (1.10) \(|\vek f| = |\vek t(Q)|\,\Delta A \le c\,\Delta A\), because \(\Delta A\) is a positive number. Therefore \(|\vek r\times\vek f| \le c\,r_{\max}\,\Delta A\).
  3. Every component of a vector is at most its length in absolute value, since for example \(q_{\mathrm{x}}^2 \le q_{\mathrm{x}}^2 + q_{\mathrm{y}}^2 + q_{\mathrm{z}}^2\), as in step 3 of the proof of Cauchy's formula (theorem 2.24).
  4. A component of the moment of the distributed force is the sum of the same components of the moments of all bits. By the triangle inequality for numbers (lemma 1.6, item 1) its absolute value is at most the sum of the absolute values, and by steps 2 and 3 this is at most \(c\,r_{\max}\) times the sum of the areas, that is, \(c\,A\,r_{\max}\).
  5. For a force distributed over a volume we repeat steps 1 to 4 with bits of volume \(\Delta V\) and forces \(\vek b(Q)\,\Delta V\).

Source: The lemma and the proof are not from the sources.

Item 1 says that an evenly distributed force turns a body as if all of it acted at the centre of the face (figure 2.44). The reason is symmetry. Every bit on one side of the centre has a partner on the other side, and the contributions of the vectors \(\vek s\) and \(-\vek s\) cancel in the sum of the moments. In section 2.7 we used the same idea of pairs of patches symmetric about the centre for the force across a face. Item 2 says that a small force per unit area on a small face near \(O\) gives a small moment.

First let us compute what the moment would be if the stress components at all points of the cube were the same as at \(P\). On the face \(x = h/2\) an evenly distributed force with the traction \((\sigma_{\mathrm{xx}}, \sigma_{\mathrm{xy}}, \sigma_{\mathrm{xz}})\) per unit area would then act. The face is a square with the area \(h^2\) and the centre \((h/2, 0, 0)\), so by item 1 of lemma 2.35 on the moment of a distributed force and by (2.32) its moment about \(P\) is

\[\Big(\frac h2, 0, 0\Big)\times h^2\,(\sigma_{\mathrm{xx}}, \sigma_{\mathrm{xy}}, \sigma_{\mathrm{xz}}) = \frac{h^3}{2}\,(0,\ -\sigma_{\mathrm{xz}},\ \sigma_{\mathrm{xy}}) .\]

On the opposite face \(x = -h/2\) both factors are opposite, the vector to the centre \((-h/2, 0, 0)\) and the force \(-h^2\,(\sigma_{\mathrm{xx}}, \sigma_{\mathrm{xy}}, \sigma_{\mathrm{xz}})\). By item 3 of lemma 2.31 on the properties of the vector product the signs cancel, \((-1)(-1) = 1\), and the moment is the same. We compute the other faces in the same way:

faces moment of each of the two faces
\(x = \pm h/2\) \(\tfrac{h^3}{2}\,(0,\ -\sigma_{\mathrm{xz}},\ \sigma_{\mathrm{xy}})\)
\(y = \pm h/2\) \(\tfrac{h^3}{2}\,(\sigma_{\mathrm{yz}},\ 0,\ -\sigma_{\mathrm{yx}})\)
\(z = \pm h/2\) \(\tfrac{h^3}{2}\,(-\sigma_{\mathrm{zy}},\ \sigma_{\mathrm{zx}},\ 0)\)

We count each row twice, once for each face, so the sum of all six moments is

\[h^3\,\big(\sigma_{\mathrm{yz}} - \sigma_{\mathrm{zy}},\ \ \sigma_{\mathrm{zx}} - \sigma_{\mathrm{xz}},\ \ \sigma_{\mathrm{xy}} - \sigma_{\mathrm{yx}}\big) . \tag{2.36}\]

The normal components \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xx}}\), \(\sigma_{\mathrm{yy}}\) and \(\sigma_{\mathrm{zz}}\) do not appear in the sum. Their forces point along the axis on which the centre of the face lies, so the line of action passes through \(P\), the lever arm is zero, and so is the moment (figure 2.45, right). Only the shear components appear. Let us look at the component \(z\). The forces \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xy}}h^2\) on the faces \(x = \pm h/2\) point in opposite directions on opposite sides of \(P\), each with the lever arm \(h/2\), and turn the cube about the axis \(z\) counterclockwise. The forces \(\sigma_{\mathrm{yx}}h^2\) on the faces \(y = \pm h/2\) turn it clockwise (figure 2.45, left and middle). The component \(z\) of the sum is zero only if the two pairs are equally strong, \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xy}} = \sigma_{\mathrm{yx}}\).

What about everything we left out? The moments in (2.36) are proportional to \(h^3\): the force is proportional to the area of the face \(h^2\) and the lever arm to half the side \(h/2\). The weight of the cube is proportional to its volume \(h^3\), and every bit of the cube is at most as far from \(P\) as a corner, \(\sqrt{3\,(h/2)^2} = \tfrac{\sqrt3}{2}\,h\). By item 2 of lemma 2.35 on the moment of a distributed force the moment of the weight is therefore at most proportional to \(h^4\). The stress components also change across the cube. For a continuously differentiable field the difference between the value at a point of a face and the value at \(P\) is at most proportional to the distance, that is, to \(h\), which we will show in the proof below. The force due to this difference is therefore proportional to \(h \cdot h^2\), and its moment to \(h \cdot h^2 \cdot h = h^4\), with the size of the cube, the area and the lever arm. When we shrink the cube, \(h^4\) decreases faster than \(h^3\).

How much faster, let us show on a steel cube with \(\rho g = 7800 \cdot 9{,}81 = 76\,518\) N/m³, as for the tetrahedron in section 2.6.2. In it the density of the weight is the same everywhere in the cube, so the moment of the weight about the centre \(P\) is in fact exactly zero. We divide the cube into equal small cubes. A small cube whose centre is shifted from \(P\) by the vector \(\vek s\) has a partner whose centre is shifted by \(-\vek s\), the same force \(\vek f\) acts on both, and by item 3 of lemma 2.31 on the properties of the vector product the sum of their moments is \(\vek s\times\vek f + (-\vek s)\times\vek f = \vek 0\), as in item 1 of lemma 2.35 on the moment of a distributed force. We need the bound of item 2 for a body force whose density varies across the cube, and the table shows how fast such a bound shrinks when the density is at most \(\rho g\) in size. Suppose \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xy}}\) were larger than \(\sigma_{\mathrm{yx}}\) by 1 MPa. By (2.36) the moment of the pairs would be \(h^3 \cdot 1\) MPa, and the bound for the moment of the body force, by the same item 2, the force \(\rho g\,h^3\) times the largest distance \(\tfrac{\sqrt3}{2}\,h\). We computed with NumPy:

\(h\) \(h^3 \cdot 1\) MPa \(\tfrac{\sqrt3}{2}\,\rho g\,h^4\) ratio
1 mm \(1 \cdot 10^{-3}\) N m \(6{,}627 \cdot 10^{-8}\) N m \(6{,}627 \cdot 10^{-5}\)
0,1 mm \(1 \cdot 10^{-6}\) N m \(6{,}627 \cdot 10^{-12}\) N m \(6{,}627 \cdot 10^{-6}\)
0,01 mm \(1 \cdot 10^{-9}\) N m \(6{,}627 \cdot 10^{-16}\) N m \(6{,}627 \cdot 10^{-7}\)

When we decrease \(h\) by a factor of 10, the moment of the pairs decreases by a factor of 1000, the bound for the moment of the body force by a factor of 10 000, and their ratio falls by a factor of 10 (figure 2.46). In a small enough cube the body force cannot balance any difference between \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xy}}\) and \(\sigma_{\mathrm{yx}}\) other than zero. The same holds for the change of stress across the cube. In the hanging bar the stress \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xx}} = \rho g\,(L - x)\) changes over the distance \(h\) by \(\rho g\,h\), for \(h = 1\) mm by \(76{,}52\) Pa, and the moment that such a change gives is again at most proportional to \(h^4\). The only possibility left is that the differences in (2.36) are zero. This is the heart of the derivation, which we now write down precisely. As with the tetrahedron, two quantities shrink together, but at different rates, and their ratio decides.

2.8.5 Symmetry of stress

We state the theorem with the assumptions we used in section 2.7. The first is that the stress components are continuously differentiable fields (definition 1.90). We will need only what theorem 1.88 on the change of a field over a short step uses of it, and we write that into the theorem. The second concerns the body force. Its density is to be bounded near \(P\). This holds for the weight, whose density has the size \(\rho g\) everywhere. It holds also for every body force density that is continuous at \(P\), since then near \(P\) each of its components differs from its value at \(P\) by less than 1 N/m³ (definition 1.67 with the error 1 N/m³). The third assumption is the way we compute the moments of distributed forces.

Theorem 2.36 Symmetry of stress (simetrija napetosti)

Let a body be in equilibrium, \(P\) a point in its interior and \(x\), \(y\), \(z\) the axes of a right-handed rectangular Cartesian coordinate system. Assume:

  1. every stress component is defined at all points that are less than some number \(r_1 > 0\) away from \(P\), has all three partial derivatives there, and these are continuous at \(P\),
  2. there are numbers \(B\) and \(r_0 > 0\) such that the body force density \(\vek b\) has a size of at most \(B\) at every point less than \(r_0\) away from \(P\),
  3. only forces across its surface and the body force act on any part of the body, and their moments are computed as sums of the moments of small forces, as in lemma 2.35 on the moment of a distributed force, where a face that is a rectangle is divided by lines parallel to its sides into equal rectangles with the points at their centres.

Then at the point \(P\)

\[\sigma_{\mathrm{xy}} = \sigma_{\mathrm{yx}} , \qquad \sigma_{\mathrm{xz}} = \sigma_{\mathrm{zx}} , \qquad \sigma_{\mathrm{yz}} = \sigma_{\mathrm{zy}} . \tag{2.37}\]
Proof

We must show that the differences \(\sigma_{\mathrm{yz}} - \sigma_{\mathrm{zy}}\), \(\sigma_{\mathrm{zx}} - \sigma_{\mathrm{xz}}\) and \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xy}} - \sigma_{\mathrm{yx}}\) at \(P\) are zero. We write the equilibrium of moments of a small cube with the centre \(P\). The moment given by the values of stress at \(P\) is proportional to \(h^3\), everything else at most proportional to \(h^4\).

  1. We put the origin at \(P\). For \(h > 0\) we take the cube with centre \(P\), side \(h\) and faces in the planes \(x = \pm h/2\), \(y = \pm h/2\) and \(z = \pm h/2\). Every point of the cube has coordinates that are at most \(h/2\) in absolute value, so by (1.10) it is at most \(\sqrt{3\,(h/2)^2} = \tfrac{\sqrt3}{2}\,h\) away from \(P\).
  2. We apply theorem 1.88 on the change of a field over a short step to the component \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xy}}\), with the error \(\eta_1 = 1\) Pa/m. Its hypotheses are assumption 1. So there is \(\delta_{\mathrm{xy}} > 0\) such that for every point \(Q\) with the vector \(\overrightarrow{PQ} = (\Delta x, \Delta y, \Delta z)\) and \(0 < |\overrightarrow{PQ}| < \delta_{\mathrm{xy}}\)
    \[\sigma_{\mathrm{xy}}(Q) - \sigma_{\mathrm{xy}}(P) = \frac{\partial\sigma_{\mathrm{xy}}}{\partial x}\,\Delta x + \frac{\partial\sigma_{\mathrm{xy}}}{\partial y}\,\Delta y + \frac{\partial\sigma_{\mathrm{xy}}}{\partial z}\,\Delta z + R , \qquad |R| \le \eta_1\,|\overrightarrow{PQ}| ,\]
    with the partial derivatives at \(P\).
  3. Each of the components \(\Delta x\), \(\Delta y\) and \(\Delta z\) is at most \(|\overrightarrow{PQ}|\) in absolute value. By the triangle inequality for numbers therefore
    \[|\sigma_{\mathrm{xy}}(Q) - \sigma_{\mathrm{xy}}(P)| \le G_{\mathrm{xy}}\,|\overrightarrow{PQ}| , \qquad G_{\mathrm{xy}} = \Big|\frac{\partial\sigma_{\mathrm{xy}}}{\partial x}\Big| + \Big|\frac{\partial\sigma_{\mathrm{xy}}}{\partial y}\Big| + \Big|\frac{\partial\sigma_{\mathrm{xy}}}{\partial z}\Big| + \eta_1 .\]
    At \(Q = P\) the inequality holds because both sides are zero.
  4. We do the same for all nine stress components. Let \(G\) be the largest of the nine numbers \(G_{\mathrm{xx}}, G_{\mathrm{xy}}, \dots, G_{\mathrm{zz}}\) and \(\delta_1\) the smallest of the nine numbers \(\delta_{\mathrm{xx}}, \delta_{\mathrm{xy}}, \dots, \delta_{\mathrm{zz}}\). For every point \(Q\) with \(|\overrightarrow{PQ}| < \delta_1\) each stress component at \(Q\) then differs from its value at \(P\) by at most \(G\,|\overrightarrow{PQ}|\).
  5. Since \(P\) is in the interior of the body, we can choose \(h\) so small that the whole cube lies in the body and that \(\tfrac{\sqrt3}{2}\,h\) is smaller than \(\delta_1\) and than \(r_0\). By step 1 the bound of step 4 and assumption 2 then hold at every point of the cube.
  6. The cube is a part of a body in equilibrium, so it is in equilibrium itself (section 2.1), and by (2.35) the sum of the moments of all forces on it about \(P\) is the zero vector. By assumption 3 these are the forces across the six faces and the body force.
  7. On the face \(x = h/2\) the outward normal is \(\vek e_{\mathrm{x}}\), and the force per unit area at its point \(Q\) is the traction vector \(\vek t(Q, \vek e_{\mathrm{x}})\) (definition 2.25). We write it as the sum \(\vek t_{\mathrm{P}} + \vek q(Q)\), where \(\vek t_{\mathrm{P}} = (\sigma_{\mathrm{xx}}, \sigma_{\mathrm{xy}}, \sigma_{\mathrm{xz}})\) with the values at \(P\), and \(\vek q(Q)\) is the difference. By steps 4 and 5 each component of the difference is at most \(G\,\tfrac{\sqrt3}{2}\,h\) in absolute value, so by (1.10) \(|\vek q(Q)| \le \sqrt3 \cdot G\,\tfrac{\sqrt3}{2}\,h = \tfrac32\,G\,h\).
  8. The force on each rectangle of the division of the face is the sum of the forces \(\vek t_{\mathrm{P}}\,\Delta A\) and \(\vek q(Q)\,\Delta A\), so by item 2 of lemma 2.31 on the properties of the vector product the moment of the force on the face is the sum of two moments. The first is the moment of the evenly distributed force \(\vek t_{\mathrm{P}}\), and by item 1 of lemma 2.35 on the moment of a distributed force it equals \(\tfrac{h^3}{2}\,(0, -\sigma_{\mathrm{xz}}, \sigma_{\mathrm{xy}})\), as in the table before the theorem. The second is the moment of the force \(\vek q\). By item 2 of the same lemma with \(c = \tfrac32\,G\,h\), \(A = h^2\) and \(r_{\max} = \tfrac{\sqrt3}{2}\,h\), each of its components is at most \(\tfrac32\,G\,h \cdot h^2 \cdot \tfrac{\sqrt3}{2}\,h = \tfrac{3\sqrt3}{4}\,G\,h^4\) in absolute value.
  9. We proceed in the same way on the other five faces. On the face \(x = -h/2\) the force per unit area is, by lemma 2.21 on the traction on the opposite side of a cut, \(-\vek t(Q, \vek e_{\mathrm{x}})\), and on the faces \(y = \pm h/2\) and \(z = \pm h/2\) it is \(\pm\vek t(Q, \vek e_{\mathrm{y}})\) and \(\pm\vek t(Q, \vek e_{\mathrm{z}})\). The moments of the even parts are in the table before the theorem, and their sum is (2.36). The moments of the differences are again at most \(\tfrac{3\sqrt3}{4}\,G\,h^4\) in each component.
  10. By step 5 the body force density has a size of at most \(B\) at every point of the cube. By item 2 of the lemma on the moment of a distributed force for the volume \(V = h^3\) and \(r_{\max} = \tfrac{\sqrt3}{2}\,h\), each component of its moment is at most \(\tfrac{\sqrt3}{2}\,B\,h^4\) in absolute value.
  11. The component \(z\) of the sum of all moments is zero. It consists of the component \(z\) of the vector (2.36), \(h^3\,(\sigma_{\mathrm{xy}} - \sigma_{\mathrm{yx}})\), the six components of the moments of the differences from steps 8 and 9, and the component of the moment of the body force from step 10. So \(h^3\,(\sigma_{\mathrm{xy}} - \sigma_{\mathrm{yx}})\) is the negative of the sum of the other seven numbers, and by the triangle inequality for numbers
    \[h^3\,|\sigma_{\mathrm{xy}} - \sigma_{\mathrm{yx}}| \le 6 \cdot \frac{3\sqrt3}{4}\,G\,h^4 + \frac{\sqrt3}{2}\,B\,h^4 = K\,h^4 , \qquad K = \frac{9\sqrt3}{2}\,G + \frac{\sqrt3}{2}\,B .\]
  12. We divide the inequality by the positive number \(h^3\) and get \(|\sigma_{\mathrm{xy}} - \sigma_{\mathrm{yx}}| \le K\,h\). This holds for every \(h > 0\) that satisfies step 5.
  13. We choose any number \(\eta > 0\). We choose \(h\) so that it satisfies step 5 and \(K\,h \le \eta\). For \(K > 0\) it is enough to require also \(h \le \eta/K\), for \(K = 0\) every \(h\) of step 5 will do. Then \(|\sigma_{\mathrm{xy}} - \sigma_{\mathrm{yx}}| \le \eta\).
  14. So the nonnegative number \(|\sigma_{\mathrm{xy}} - \sigma_{\mathrm{yx}}|\) is not larger than any positive number \(\eta\). By lemma 1.34 on an inequality tested with all positive numbers it is zero, and \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xy}} = \sigma_{\mathrm{yx}}\).
  15. The components \(x\) and \(y\) of the sum of the moments give, by the same steps, \(|\sigma_{\mathrm{yz}} - \sigma_{\mathrm{zy}}| \le K\,h\) and \(|\sigma_{\mathrm{zx}} - \sigma_{\mathrm{xz}}| \le K\,h\), so also \(\sigma_{\mathrm{yz}} = \sigma_{\mathrm{zy}}\) and \(\sigma_{\mathrm{zx}} = \sigma_{\mathrm{xz}}\).

Source: SADD (3.7.7) (PDF p. 79), CM (5.3.31) (PDF p. 234), EP (2.2.17) (p. 54), BOWER §2.3.2 (PDF p. 78). SADD, CM and BOWER derive the theorem from the equilibrium of moments on a finite part of the body with integrals, EP with moments on a small box, much as we do. The proof with bounds is not from the sources.

Next to Cauchy's formula, this is the second result on which the whole theory of stress rests, so let us remember it. The proof showed why it holds. The shear forces on opposite faces of a small cube form pairs that turn the cube, and the moment of each pair is proportional to the area of the face and to the lever arm, that is, to \(h^3\). Everything else, the body force and the change of stress across the cube, gives moments at most proportional to \(h^4\). In a small cube the pairs of shear forces must therefore balance each other. The idea is the same as with the tetrahedron in section 2.6.2, where the weight disappeared because it shrank faster than the forces across the faces.

What does the theorem mean for the material? A shear component never appears alone. When a shear component in the direction of the axis \(y\) acts on the face with the normal \(\vek e_{\mathrm{x}}\), an equally large shear component in the direction of the axis \(x\) acts on the face with the normal \(\vek e_{\mathrm{y}}\) through the same point. In figure 2.45 the forces on the left and in the middle must therefore be equally large, and the cube does not turn.

Where does the theorem fail? Assumption 3 excludes bodies on which, besides forces, distributed moments act that are not moments of forces. CM and EP call them body couples (telesni momenti) and say that without them the second condition of equilibrium gives the symmetry of stress (CM §5.3.3, PDF pp. 232-234, EP §2.2.2, p. 54). For materials whose inner structure carries such moments too, CM writes additional equations (CM §5.3.3.2, PDF p. 234). We do not treat such materials in this book. Assumption 1 excludes points at which the stress changes by a jump. We proved the theorem for a body in equilibrium. CM derives the symmetry also for a body that moves (CM (5.3.28)-(5.3.31), PDF pp. 233-234), much as in Cauchy's formula the term with the acceleration disappeared in the same way as the weight.

2.8.6 Pure shear again

Let us return to the cube in pure shear of section 2.6.6 (figure 2.28). The cube has the side \(s\), the axis \(x\) points to the right, the axis \(z\) up, and the axis \(y\) into the picture, away from the viewer, so that the system is right-handed. We pull the top face to the right and the bottom face to the left with the force \(\tau_0\) per unit area. We pull the right face up and the left face down, now with the force \(\tau_1\) per unit area, and ask how large \(\tau_1\) must be. The first condition of equilibrium does not tell, since for every \(\tau_1\) the forces on the top and the bottom face are opposite, and so are the forces on the side faces.

The forces are distributed evenly over the faces, so by item 1 of lemma 2.35 on the moment of a distributed force each of them turns the cube as if it acted at the centre of its face. We put the origin at the centre \(P\) of the cube (figure 2.47). The force on the top face is \(\tau_0 s^2\,\vek e_{\mathrm{x}}\) at the point \((0, 0, s/2)\), on the bottom face \(-\tau_0 s^2\,\vek e_{\mathrm{x}}\) at the point \((0, 0, -s/2)\), on the right face \(\tau_1 s^2\,\vek e_{\mathrm{z}}\) at the point \((s/2, 0, 0)\) and on the left face \(-\tau_1 s^2\,\vek e_{\mathrm{z}}\) at the point \((-s/2, 0, 0)\). By (2.32) their moments about \(P\) are

\[\begin{aligned} \Big(0, 0, \frac s2\Big)\times(\tau_0 s^2, 0, 0) &= \Big(0,\ \frac{\tau_0 s^3}{2},\ 0\Big) , \\ \Big(0, 0, -\frac s2\Big)\times(-\tau_0 s^2, 0, 0) &= \Big(0,\ \frac{\tau_0 s^3}{2},\ 0\Big) , \\ \Big(\frac s2, 0, 0\Big)\times(0, 0, \tau_1 s^2) &= \Big(0,\ -\frac{\tau_1 s^3}{2},\ 0\Big) , \\ \Big(-\frac s2, 0, 0\Big)\times(0, 0, -\tau_1 s^2) &= \Big(0,\ -\frac{\tau_1 s^3}{2},\ 0\Big) . \end{aligned}\]

The sum is \(\big(0,\ (\tau_0 - \tau_1)\,s^3,\ 0\big)\). The second condition of equilibrium (2.35) requires it to be zero, so \(\tau_1 = \tau_0\). This is what we promised in section 2.6.6: the cube is in equilibrium exactly when all four forces per unit area are equally large. The moment of the pair on the top and the bottom face points in the direction of the axis \(y\), into the picture, and the viewer sees the cube turn clockwise. The moment of the pair on the side faces points out of the picture, and this pair turns the cube the other way. For \(\tau_0 = 50\) MPa and \(s = 10\) mm the force on the top face is \(\tau_0 s^2 = 50 \cdot 10^6\ \text{Pa} \cdot 10^{-4}\ \text{m}^2 = 5000\) N, and the moment of the pair is \(\tau_0 s^3 = 50 \cdot 10^6\ \text{Pa} \cdot 10^{-6}\ \text{m}^3 = 50\) N m. Without the forces on the side faces a moment of 50 N m would turn the cube.

In terms of stress components, \(\tau_0 = \sigma_{\mathrm{zx}}\), the component \(x\) of the traction on the face with the normal \(\vek e_{\mathrm{z}}\), and \(\tau_1 = \sigma_{\mathrm{xz}}\), the component \(z\) of the traction on the face with the normal \(\vek e_{\mathrm{x}}\). The condition \(\tau_1 = \tau_0\) is therefore \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xz}} = \sigma_{\mathrm{zx}}\), the symmetry of stress (2.37) in this example. On the ruler, two forces with zero resultant formed a pair that turns the ruler. On the cube in pure shear there are two such pairs, and they balance each other.

Theorem 2.36 on the symmetry of stress says that among the nine stress components at a point at most six are different: three normal ones, \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xx}}\), \(\sigma_{\mathrm{yy}}\) and \(\sigma_{\mathrm{zz}}\), and three shear ones, \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xy}} = \sigma_{\mathrm{yx}}\), \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xz}} = \sigma_{\mathrm{zx}}\) and \(\sigma_{\mathrm{yz}} = \sigma_{\mathrm{zy}}\) (SADD, PDF p. 79, EP, p. 54). The same is true of strain, which at a point is described by six numbers (definition 1.115). The reason, though, is different. For strain, \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xy}} = \varepsilon_{\mathrm{yx}}\) holds by definition, because both are half of the same sum \(\partial u_{\mathrm{x}}/\partial y + \partial u_{\mathrm{y}}/\partial x\). For stress, \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xy}}\) and \(\sigma_{\mathrm{yx}}\) are components of forces on two different faces, and they are equal because of a law of mechanics, the second condition of equilibrium.

The table of the nine numbers of section 2.6.5, in which each row is one traction vector, is therefore symmetric about the diagonal:

\[\begin{array}{c|ccc} & x & y & z \\ \hline \vek t(\vek e_{\mathrm{x}}) & \sigma_{\mathrm{xx}} & \sigma_{\mathrm{xy}} & \sigma_{\mathrm{xz}} \\ \vek t(\vek e_{\mathrm{y}}) & \sigma_{\mathrm{xy}} & \sigma_{\mathrm{yy}} & \sigma_{\mathrm{yz}} \\ \vek t(\vek e_{\mathrm{z}}) & \sigma_{\mathrm{xz}} & \sigma_{\mathrm{yz}} & \sigma_{\mathrm{zz}} \end{array}\]

As a matrix (definition 1.93) it equals its transposed matrix, so it is symmetric (definition 1.102). For Cauchy's formula this means a simplification. By (2.24) we got the component \(x\) of the traction vector \(\vek t(\vek n)\) from the column \(x\) of the table, \(t_{\mathrm{x}}(\vek n) = \sigma_{\mathrm{xx}}\,n_{\mathrm{x}} + \sigma_{\mathrm{yx}}\,n_{\mathrm{y}} + \sigma_{\mathrm{zx}}\,n_{\mathrm{z}}\). Because of the symmetry the column equals the row of the same name, and

\[\begin{aligned} t_{\mathrm{x}}(\vek n) &= \sigma_{\mathrm{xx}}\,n_{\mathrm{x}} + \sigma_{\mathrm{xy}}\,n_{\mathrm{y}} + \sigma_{\mathrm{xz}}\,n_{\mathrm{z}} , \\ t_{\mathrm{y}}(\vek n) &= \sigma_{\mathrm{xy}}\,n_{\mathrm{x}} + \sigma_{\mathrm{yy}}\,n_{\mathrm{y}} + \sigma_{\mathrm{yz}}\,n_{\mathrm{z}} , \\ t_{\mathrm{z}}(\vek n) &= \sigma_{\mathrm{xz}}\,n_{\mathrm{x}} + \sigma_{\mathrm{yz}}\,n_{\mathrm{y}} + \sigma_{\mathrm{zz}}\,n_{\mathrm{z}} . \end{aligned}\]

With this the difference between our order of indices and that of CM, which exchanges the two indices (section 2.6.5), also disappears, since exchanging the indices does not change a stress component.

Of the three questions at the end of section 2.6.6 we have answered the last. The first two remain: how the six numbers change when we turn the axes, and on which face through the point the normal stress is largest. We take up the first in the next section, where we write the table of stress as a matrix and use it to turn the axes.

2.9 Turned axes

At the end of section 2.6 three questions were left open. The last one, how the second condition of equilibrium relates \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xy}}\) and \(\sigma_{\mathrm{yx}}\), was answered by section 2.8: the two components are equal. Now we take up the first one, how the stress components change when we turn the axes. The second, on which face through the point the normal stress is largest, will wait for section 2.11. The stress components at a point \(P\) are the components of three traction vectors on the faces through \(P\) that are perpendicular to the axes of the coordinate system. If we turn the axes, these are three other faces, other traction vectors act on them, and we split each of them along other axes. How do we compute the nine numbers in the new axes from the nine numbers in the old ones?

The question is not only one of computation. In the bar of section 2.4 only a normal stress acted on the cross section, but on an oblique cut there was also a shear stress, and for steel it is the shear stress that decides when yielding begins. In the pure shear of section 2.6.6 only shear stresses acted on the faces of the cube, but on the diagonal faces only tension and compression. In a plate reinforced with fibres we want the stress on faces along the fibres and across them, not on faces along the edges of the plate (CM Example 4.3.1, PDF p. 186). We place the axes where the computation is easiest, but we need the stress on faces that the material and the structure choose.

The goal of this section is the rule that gives the components in one rectangular Cartesian coordinate system from the components in another. We will derive it first for vectors, then for stress and for strain. Stress and strain will turn out to have the same rule, and this very rule will say exactly what the word means with which books name such quantities. Along the way we will write Cauchy's formula with matrices and show how the shear strain measures the change of a right angle, which in chapter 1 we only announced.

What do we assume? Both coordinate systems are rectangular Cartesian, with the same unit of length, and their origins are at the same point. The last is no restriction. The components of a vector are differences of coordinates ((1.8)), and if we move the origin without turning the axes, the coordinates of all points change by the same three numbers, while their differences stay. We assume nothing about the body or the material. What we derive for stress holds at every point where Cauchy's formula holds, that is, at every interior point of a body in equilibrium at which the average forces per unit area approach the traction vector (theorem 2.24). From section 2.3 we will use the fact that the length of a vector and the scalar product of two vectors are the same numbers in every rectangular Cartesian coordinate system with the same unit. The symmetry of the stress components (theorem 2.36) we will need in one place only, and we will say where. For strain we assume, as in section 1.17, a continuously differentiable displacement field (definition 1.90) and small partial derivatives of the displacements.

2.9.1 The rotation matrix

In section 1.5.5 we turned the axes by a quarter turn about the axis \(z\) and found that the flight of the fly, which had the components \((1, 2, -2)\) in the old axes, has the components \((2, -1, -2)\) in the new axes. We got there by thinking about how many steps along which new axis make up the flight. For an arbitrary turn such thinking is no longer simple, so we need a rule.

The question of how to get the coordinates of a point in one rectangular system from its coordinates in another system with the same origin is older than matrices. MUIR counts it among the problems of coordinate geometry (MUIR, PDF p. 433). As the first paper on his list of papers about it he gives Euler's book Introductio in analysin infinitorum of 1748, more precisely its appendix on surfaces (MUIR, PDF p. 433). The list also contains papers on the rotation of a body, among them Lagrange's of 1773 (MUIR, PDF p. 434). In a rotating body the axes attached to it turn relative to the axes at rest, and this is exactly our problem. Expressions in the coefficients of equations, which we shall meet in section 2.10, appeared in attempts to solve this problem only comparatively late. For a change of coordinates does not reduce to mere elimination of unknowns from a system of linear equations (MUIR, PDF p. 433).

We name the new axes \(\bar x\), \(\bar y\) and \(\bar z\) and their unit vectors \(\bar{\vek e}_{\mathrm{x}}\), \(\bar{\vek e}_{\mathrm{y}}\) and \(\bar{\vek e}_{\mathrm{z}}\), as in section 1.5.5. The new axes, too, are the axes of a rectangular Cartesian coordinate system: they are mutually perpendicular, and lengths on them are measured with the same unit as on the old ones. So \(\bar{\vek e}_{\mathrm{x}}\), \(\bar{\vek e}_{\mathrm{y}}\) and \(\bar{\vek e}_{\mathrm{z}}\) are three unit vectors that are pairwise perpendicular. We can write each of them with components in the old system, like any other vector. For the quarter turn they are

\[\bar{\vek e}_{\mathrm{x}} = (0, 1, 0) , \qquad \bar{\vek e}_{\mathrm{y}} = (-1, 0, 0) , \qquad \bar{\vek e}_{\mathrm{z}} = (0, 0, 1) .\]

For a turn about the axis \(z\) by another angle, let us take \(\bar{\vek e}_{\mathrm{x}} = (c, s, 0)\), where \(c\) and \(s\) are numbers with \(c^2 + s^2 = 1\), so that the vector is a unit vector. For \(\bar{\vek e}_{\mathrm{y}}\) we take \((-s, c, 0)\). This vector is a unit vector too, because \(s^2 + c^2 = 1\), and it is perpendicular to \(\bar{\vek e}_{\mathrm{x}}\), because \(c\,(-s) + s\,c + 0 \cdot 0 = 0\). The axis \(z\) stays as it is, \(\bar{\vek e}_{\mathrm{z}} = (0, 0, 1)\), and this vector is perpendicular to both previous ones, because their component \(z\) is zero. With \(c = 0\) and \(s = 1\) we get the quarter turn from above. We have met both vectors before. In section 2.4, \(\vek n = (\cos\theta, \sin\theta, 0)\) was the unit normal of the oblique cut of the bar and \(\vek d = (-\sin\theta, \cos\theta, 0)\) the direction in the cut. So the numbers \(c\) and \(s\) are the cosine and the sine of the angle \(\theta\) by which the new axis \(x\) is turned from the old one toward the axis \(y\) (figure 2.48). We will not need the angle itself, the numbers \(c\) and \(s\) are enough. In the examples we take \(c = 0{,}6\) and \(s = 0{,}8\), for which \(c^2 + s^2 = 0{,}36 + 0{,}64 = 1\). This corresponds to the angle \(\theta = 53{,}13^\circ\).

We collect the nine components of the new unit vectors in a matrix, one vector in each row.

Definition 2.37 Rotation matrix (matrika zasuka)

Let two rectangular Cartesian coordinate systems with the same unit of length be given, an old system with the unit vectors of the axes \(\vek e_{\mathrm{x}}\), \(\vek e_{\mathrm{y}}\), \(\vek e_{\mathrm{z}}\) and a new system with the unit vectors of the axes \(\bar{\vek e}_{\mathrm{x}}\), \(\bar{\vek e}_{\mathrm{y}}\), \(\bar{\vek e}_{\mathrm{z}}\). The rotation matrix (matrika zasuka) is the \(3 \times 3\) matrix \(\mat Q\) whose row \(k\) holds the components of the vector \(\bar{\vek e}_{\mathrm{k}}\) in the old system:

\[Q_{\mathrm{kj}} = \bar{\vek e}_{\mathrm{k}}\cdot\vek e_{\mathrm{j}} , \tag{2.38}\]

where the indices \(k\) and \(j\) run over \(x\), \(y\) and \(z\). The numbers \(Q_{\mathrm{kj}}\) are the direction cosines (smerni kosinusi) of the new axes with respect to the old ones.

Source: CM (2.2.71), (2.2.72) (PDF pp. 58-59), where the matrix is written \([L]\) with the entries \(\ell_{\mathrm{ij}}\), SADD (1.4.1) (PDF p. 16), where it is written \(Q_{\mathrm{ij}}\).

What do these numbers mean? The entry \(Q_{\mathrm{kj}}\) is the component \(j\) of the vector \(\bar{\vek e}_{\mathrm{k}}\) in the old system. By section 2.3 the component of a vector along the old axis \(j\) is its projection onto \(\vek e_{\mathrm{j}}\), so \(Q_{\mathrm{kj}} = \bar{\vek e}_{\mathrm{k}}\cdot\vek e_{\mathrm{j}}\), as (2.38) says. For the angle \(\varphi\) between nonzero vectors \(\vek a\) and \(\vek b\), \(\cos\varphi = \vek a\cdot\vek b/(|\vek a|\,|\vek b|)\) (KREYSZIG §9.2 (4), PDF p. 388, section 2.3). The vectors \(\bar{\vek e}_{\mathrm{k}}\) and \(\vek e_{\mathrm{j}}\) are unit vectors, so their scalar product is the cosine of the angle between the new axis \(k\) and the old axis \(j\). Hence the name direction cosines. For the turn about the axis \(z\),

\[\mat Q = \begin{bmatrix} c & s & 0 \\ -s & c & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix} , \qquad \text{and for } c = 0{,}6 \text{ and } s = 0{,}8 \qquad \mat Q = \begin{bmatrix} 0{,}6 & 0{,}8 & 0 \\ -0{,}8 & 0{,}6 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix} .\]

The entry \(Q_{\mathrm{xx}} = c = \cos\theta\) is the cosine of the angle \(\theta\) between the axes \(\bar x\) and \(x\). The entry \(Q_{\mathrm{xy}} = s = \sin\theta\) is the cosine of the angle \(90^\circ - \theta\) between the axes \(\bar x\) and \(y\), since \(\cos(90^\circ - \theta) = \sin\theta\) (school trigonometry, as in section 2.4). CM writes the same matrix for plates with fibres turned by the angle \(\theta\) (CM (4.3.5), PDF p. 187).

Why the name rotation? We usually get the new system by turning the old one. The definition, however, also covers a new system in which the opposite positive direction is chosen on some axis, as in item 2 of the proof of Cauchy's formula (theorem 2.24). With the axis \(x\) reversed, for example, \(\bar{\vek e}_{\mathrm{x}} = (-1, 0, 0)\). Such a system is not only turned but also mirrored. Everything we derive holds in both cases. CM keeps the name rotation (zasuk) for the case without mirroring (CM §2.3.7, PDF p. 68), and in section 2.10 we will see how the two cases are told apart by a single number.

How do we get the components of a vector in the new axes? The component of a vector along an axis is its projection onto the unit vector of that axis. So the new component \(\bar a_{\mathrm{x}}\) is the scalar product \(\vek a\cdot\bar{\vek e}_{\mathrm{x}}\). The scalar product, however, has the same value in every rectangular Cartesian system, so we may compute it with the components in the old system, which we know. This is the whole idea of the next lemma.

Lemma 2.38 Components of a vector in turned axes (komponente vektorja v zasukanih oseh)

Let two rectangular Cartesian coordinate systems with the same unit of length be given, and let \(\mat Q\) be the rotation matrix from the old one to the new one. Let a vector \(\vek a\) have the components \(a_{\mathrm{x}}\), \(a_{\mathrm{y}}\), \(a_{\mathrm{z}}\) in the old system and \(\bar a_{\mathrm{x}}\), \(\bar a_{\mathrm{y}}\), \(\bar a_{\mathrm{z}}\) in the new one. Then:

  1. \(\bar a_{\mathrm{k}} = \vek a\cdot\bar{\vek e}_{\mathrm{k}} = \sum_{\mathrm{j}} Q_{\mathrm{kj}}\,a_{\mathrm{j}}\) for \(k = x, y, z\), in short
    \[\bar{\vek a} = \mat Q\,\vek a , \tag{2.39}\]
  2. \(a_{\mathrm{j}} = \sum_{\mathrm{k}} Q_{\mathrm{kj}}\,\bar a_{\mathrm{k}}\) for \(j = x, y, z\), in short \(\vek a = \mat Q^\T\,\bar{\vek a}\).

Here \(\vek a\) and \(\bar{\vek a}\) mean the columns of components of the same vector in the old and in the new system, and the sums run over \(x\), \(y\) and \(z\).

Proof

We must show that every new component is the sum of item 1 and every old component the sum of item 2. Both times we compute the same scalar product in two systems.

  1. In the new system the unit vector \(\bar{\vek e}_{\mathrm{x}}\) has the components \((1, 0, 0)\) (definition 1.20, applied in the new system). By (2.6), computed in the new system, \(\vek a\cdot\bar{\vek e}_{\mathrm{x}} = \bar a_{\mathrm{x}} \cdot 1 + \bar a_{\mathrm{y}} \cdot 0 + \bar a_{\mathrm{z}} \cdot 0 = \bar a_{\mathrm{x}}\). Likewise \(\vek a\cdot\bar{\vek e}_{\mathrm{y}} = \bar a_{\mathrm{y}}\) and \(\vek a\cdot\bar{\vek e}_{\mathrm{z}} = \bar a_{\mathrm{z}}\).
  2. The scalar product has the same value in every rectangular Cartesian system with the same unit, because the formula \(\vek a\cdot\vek b = \tfrac12\left(|\vek a|^2 + |\vek b|^2 - |\vek b - \vek a|^2\right)\) of section 2.3 expresses it by lengths only. So we may also compute the number \(\vek a\cdot\bar{\vek e}_{\mathrm{k}}\) with the components in the old system.
  3. In the old system \(\vek a = (a_{\mathrm{x}}, a_{\mathrm{y}}, a_{\mathrm{z}})\), and by definition 2.37 of the rotation matrix \(\bar{\vek e}_{\mathrm{k}} = (Q_{\mathrm{kx}}, Q_{\mathrm{ky}}, Q_{\mathrm{kz}})\). By (2.6), \(\vek a\cdot\bar{\vek e}_{\mathrm{k}} = Q_{\mathrm{kx}}\,a_{\mathrm{x}} + Q_{\mathrm{ky}}\,a_{\mathrm{y}} + Q_{\mathrm{kz}}\,a_{\mathrm{z}} = \sum_{\mathrm{j}} Q_{\mathrm{kj}}\,a_{\mathrm{j}}\). Together with step 1 this is item 1.
  4. By (1.38) the three equations for \(k = x, y, z\) are the three components of the product \(\mat Q\,\vek a\) (definition 1.96). This is (2.39).
  5. For item 2 we swap the roles of the systems. By steps 1 and 2, applied to the vector \(\vek e_{\mathrm{j}}\), the old unit vector \(\vek e_{\mathrm{j}}\) has in the new system the components \(\vek e_{\mathrm{j}}\cdot\bar{\vek e}_{\mathrm{x}}\), \(\vek e_{\mathrm{j}}\cdot\bar{\vek e}_{\mathrm{y}}\), \(\vek e_{\mathrm{j}}\cdot\bar{\vek e}_{\mathrm{z}}\). The scalar product is symmetric (lemma 2.12, item 1), so these are the numbers \(Q_{\mathrm{xj}}\), \(Q_{\mathrm{yj}}\), \(Q_{\mathrm{zj}}\), the column \(j\) of the matrix \(\mat Q\).
  6. As in steps 1 to 3, only with the systems swapped, \(a_{\mathrm{j}} = \vek a\cdot\vek e_{\mathrm{j}}\), and when we compute this scalar product with the components in the new system we get \(a_{\mathrm{j}} = \bar a_{\mathrm{x}}\,Q_{\mathrm{xj}} + \bar a_{\mathrm{y}}\,Q_{\mathrm{yj}} + \bar a_{\mathrm{z}}\,Q_{\mathrm{zj}} = \sum_{\mathrm{k}} Q_{\mathrm{kj}}\,\bar a_{\mathrm{k}}\).
  7. By definition 1.100 of the transposed matrix, the number \(Q_{\mathrm{kj}}\) is the entry in row \(j\) and column \(k\) of the matrix \(\mat Q^\T\), so by (1.38) the sum of step 6 is the component \(j\) of the product \(\mat Q^\T\bar{\vek a}\).

Source: CM (2.2.70) (PDF p. 58), SADD (1.4.6), (1.4.7) (PDF p. 17). The sources derive the rule from writing the unit vectors of one system with the unit vectors of the other. The proof with the scalar product is not from the sources.

The proof showed that every new component is the projection onto a new unit vector, computed with the old components. Let us test the lemma on the flight of the fly \(\vek a = (1, 2, -2)\). For the quarter turn, by (1.38),

\[\mat Q\,\vek a = \begin{bmatrix} 0 & 1 & 0 \\ -1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ 2 \\ -2 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 0 \cdot 1 + 1 \cdot 2 + 0 \cdot (-2) \\ (-1) \cdot 1 + 0 \cdot 2 + 0 \cdot (-2) \\ 0 \cdot 1 + 0 \cdot 2 + 1 \cdot (-2) \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 2 \\ -1 \\ -2 \end{bmatrix} ,\]

which is what we found in section 1.5.5 by thinking. For the turn with \(c = 0{,}6\) and \(s = 0{,}8\),

\[\bar a_{\mathrm{x}} = 0{,}6 \cdot 1 + 0{,}8 \cdot 2 = 2{,}2 , \qquad \bar a_{\mathrm{y}} = -0{,}8 \cdot 1 + 0{,}6 \cdot 2 = 0{,}4 , \qquad \bar a_{\mathrm{z}} = -2 ,\]

so in the new axes the flight has the components \((\tfrac{11}{5}, \tfrac25, -2)\) (figure 2.49). Its length is \(\sqrt{2{,}2^2 + 0{,}4^2 + 2^2} = \sqrt{4{,}84 + 0{,}16 + 4} = \sqrt 9 = 3\) m, the same as in the old axes, since the arrow is the same. Item 2 gives back the old components: \(a_{\mathrm{x}} = 0{,}6 \cdot 2{,}2 - 0{,}8 \cdot 0{,}4 = 1{,}32 - 0{,}32 = 1\) and \(a_{\mathrm{y}} = 0{,}8 \cdot 2{,}2 + 0{,}6 \cdot 0{,}4 = 1{,}76 + 0{,}24 = 2\).

The lemma holds only between rectangular Cartesian systems, where a component is the projection onto the unit vector of the axis. For the oblique axes of section 1.5.1 the components are not projections, and the rule is different (CM §2.2.4, PDF pp. 48-52).

The rule for the way back has the transposed matrix. When we translate components into the new system and then back, we must get the original ones, so we expect \(\mat Q^\T\) to be the inverse matrix of \(\mat Q\). Matrices with this property have a name.

Definition 2.39 Orthogonal matrix (ortogonalna matrika)

A square matrix \(\mat Q\) is orthogonal (ortogonalna) if

\[\mat Q^\T\mat Q = \mat Q\,\mat Q^\T = \mat I . \tag{2.40}\]

Source: CM (2.3.15) (PDF p. 68), SADD (1.4.9), (1.4.10) (PDF p. 17).

A square matrix is a matrix with as many rows as columns, and the definition holds for every size. By definition 1.107 of the inverse matrix, equation (2.40) says that the transposed matrix is the inverse, \(\mat Q^{-1} = \mat Q^\T\). The name says what the equation means for the rows. The entry in row \(k\) and column \(l\) of the product \(\mat Q\,\mat Q^\T\) is \(\sum_{\mathrm{j}} Q_{\mathrm{kj}}\,Q_{\mathrm{lj}}\), the sum of the products of corresponding entries of the rows \(k\) and \(l\), and the equation requires this sum to be \(1\) for \(k = l\) and \(0\) for \(k \neq l\). So the rows are pairwise perpendicular in the sense of definition 2.11, orthogonal, and each has length \(1\). The equation \(\mat Q^\T\mat Q = \mat I\) says the same for the columns. The names orthogonal transformation (ortogonalna preobrazba) and orthogonal substitution (ortogonalna zamenjava) for the passage to new variables with such a matrix go back to 1852, both in the papers of Sylvester (MUIR, PDF p. 842).

Lemma 2.40 Orthogonality of the rotation matrix (ortogonalnost matrike zasuka)

The rotation matrix \(\mat Q\) is orthogonal. Its rows are the components of the new unit vectors of the axes in the old system, and its columns are the components of the old unit vectors of the axes in the new system.

Proof

We must show both equalities in (2.40). We write every entry of the product as the scalar product of two unit vectors.

  1. By definitions 1.98 and 1.100 the entry \((k, l)\) of the product \(\mat Q\,\mat Q^\T\) is \(\sum_{\mathrm{j}} Q_{\mathrm{kj}}\,(\mat Q^\T)_{\mathrm{jl}} = \sum_{\mathrm{j}} Q_{\mathrm{kj}}\,Q_{\mathrm{lj}}\).
  2. By definition 2.37 the rows \(k\) and \(l\) are the components of the vectors \(\bar{\vek e}_{\mathrm{k}}\) and \(\bar{\vek e}_{\mathrm{l}}\) in the old system, so by (2.6) the sum of step 1 equals \(\bar{\vek e}_{\mathrm{k}}\cdot\bar{\vek e}_{\mathrm{l}}\).
  3. The new unit vectors are unit vectors and pairwise perpendicular. So \(\bar{\vek e}_{\mathrm{k}}\cdot\bar{\vek e}_{\mathrm{k}} = |\bar{\vek e}_{\mathrm{k}}|^2 = 1\) (lemma 2.12, item 4) and \(\bar{\vek e}_{\mathrm{k}}\cdot\bar{\vek e}_{\mathrm{l}} = 0\) for \(k \neq l\) (definition 2.11). These are exactly the entries of the identity matrix (definition 1.105), so \(\mat Q\,\mat Q^\T = \mat I\).
  4. By step 5 of the proof of lemma 2.38 on the components of a vector in turned axes, the column \(j\) of the matrix \(\mat Q\) is the triple of components of the vector \(\vek e_{\mathrm{j}}\) in the new system.
  5. The entry \((i, j)\) of the product \(\mat Q^\T\mat Q\) is \(\sum_{\mathrm{k}} Q_{\mathrm{ki}}\,Q_{\mathrm{kj}}\), the sum of the products of corresponding entries of the columns \(i\) and \(j\). By step 4 and by (2.6), computed in the new system, this is \(\vek e_{\mathrm{i}}\cdot\vek e_{\mathrm{j}}\).
  6. The old unit vectors are unit vectors and pairwise perpendicular as well, so, as in step 3, \(\mat Q^\T\mat Q = \mat I\).

Source: SADD (1.4.9), (1.4.10) (PDF p. 17), CM (2.5.20) (PDF p. 87). SADD derives the equalities from the two rules for components. The proof with the scalar products of rows and columns is not from the sources.

Let us test it for \(c = 0{,}6\) and \(s = 0{,}8\). The sum of the squares of the entries of the first row is \(0{,}36 + 0{,}64 + 0 = 1\), and the sum of the products of corresponding entries of the first and the second row is \(0{,}6 \cdot (-0{,}8) + 0{,}8 \cdot 0{,}6 + 0 \cdot 0 = 0\). The lemma also tells why the rule for the way back has the transposed matrix: item 2 of lemma 2.38 is \(\vek a = \mat Q^\T\bar{\vek a} = \mat Q^{-1}\bar{\vek a}\), the rule that undoes the rule of item 1.

The converse holds too. If \(\mat Q\) is any orthogonal \(3 \times 3\) matrix, then by what we just said its rows are three pairwise perpendicular unit vectors. Drawn from the origin, they determine three perpendicular axes with the same unit of length, that is, a new rectangular Cartesian coordinate system, and \(\mat Q\) is its rotation matrix.

2.9.2 Cauchy's formula with matrices

At the end of section 2.6.5 we wrote the nine stress components in a table in which each row is one traction vector. In section 2.8.6 we already read this table as a matrix (definition 1.93) and saw that it is symmetric. Now we use it to write Cauchy's formula as the product of a matrix and a vector.

Definition 2.41 Stress matrix (matrika napetosti)

The stress matrix (matrika napetosti) \(\ten\sigma\) at a point \(P\) is the matrix of the stress components at \(P\) in a chosen rectangular Cartesian coordinate system, in which row \(i\) holds the components of the traction vector \(\vek t(\vek e_{\mathrm{i}})\):

\[\ten\sigma = \begin{bmatrix} \sigma_{\mathrm{xx}} & \sigma_{\mathrm{xy}} & \sigma_{\mathrm{xz}} \\ \sigma_{\mathrm{yx}} & \sigma_{\mathrm{yy}} & \sigma_{\mathrm{yz}} \\ \sigma_{\mathrm{zx}} & \sigma_{\mathrm{zy}} & \sigma_{\mathrm{zz}} \end{bmatrix} . \tag{2.41}\]

Source: SADD (3.2.3) (PDF p. 65), BOWER §2.2.3 (PDF pp. 70-71). CM (4.2.11) (PDF p. 183) writes the transposed matrix.

The stress matrix is a record of the stress at a point in a chosen coordinate system, just as the triple of components is a record of a vector. When we turn the axes, the matrix changes, but the stress at the point stays the same. How the matrix changes we will derive in section 2.9.3. First let us write Cauchy's formula.

  1. By (2.24) the component \(x\) of the traction vector \(\vek t(\vek n)\) is \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xx}}\,n_{\mathrm{x}} + \sigma_{\mathrm{yx}}\,n_{\mathrm{y}} + \sigma_{\mathrm{zx}}\,n_{\mathrm{z}}\). The numbers \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xx}}\), \(\sigma_{\mathrm{yx}}\), \(\sigma_{\mathrm{zx}}\) are the column \(x\) of the matrix \(\ten\sigma\).
  2. By definition 1.100 of the transposed matrix, the column \(x\) of the matrix \(\ten\sigma\) is the row \(x\) of the matrix \(\ten\sigma^\T\). So by (1.38) the sum of step 1 is the component \(x\) of the product \(\ten\sigma^\T\vek n\).
  3. The same holds for the components \(y\) and \(z\), so
    \[\vek t(\vek n) = \ten\sigma^\T\vek n , \qquad \begin{bmatrix} t_{\mathrm{x}} \\ t_{\mathrm{y}} \\ t_{\mathrm{z}} \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} \sigma_{\mathrm{xx}} & \sigma_{\mathrm{yx}} & \sigma_{\mathrm{zx}} \\ \sigma_{\mathrm{xy}} & \sigma_{\mathrm{yy}} & \sigma_{\mathrm{zy}} \\ \sigma_{\mathrm{xz}} & \sigma_{\mathrm{yz}} & \sigma_{\mathrm{zz}} \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} n_{\mathrm{x}} \\ n_{\mathrm{y}} \\ n_{\mathrm{z}} \end{bmatrix} .\]
  4. By theorem 2.36 on the symmetry of stress, \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xy}} = \sigma_{\mathrm{yx}}\), \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xz}} = \sigma_{\mathrm{zx}}\) and \(\sigma_{\mathrm{yz}} = \sigma_{\mathrm{zy}}\). So the stress matrix is symmetric (definition 1.102), \(\ten\sigma^\T = \ten\sigma\), and
    \[\vek t(\vek n) = \ten\sigma\,\vek n . \tag{2.42}\]

We used the symmetry only in step 4. The formula \(\vek t(\vek n) = \ten\sigma^\T\vek n\) holds without it too. CM writes \(\vek t = \ten\sigma\cdot\hat{\vek n}\) and in matrix form \(\{t\} = [\sigma]\{n\}\) (CM (4.2.10), (4.2.11), PDF p. 183), because its stress matrix is our matrix \(\ten\sigma^\T\). BOWER, who writes the indices as we do, writes \(\vek t(\vek n) = \vek n\cdot\ten\sigma\) and warns that because of the symmetry there is no difference between the two conventions (BOWER, PDF pp. 70-71). The difference becomes important for measures of stress that are not symmetric. We will meet them in section 2.13.

From the matrix form we also get the normal and the shear stress on a face with the unit normal \(\vek n\). By definition 2.18 the normal stress is \(\sigma_{\mathrm{n}} = \vek t\cdot\vek n\). The component \(i\) of the vector \(\ten\sigma\vek n\) is \(\sum_{\mathrm{j}} \sigma_{\mathrm{ij}}\,n_{\mathrm{j}}\), so \(\sigma_{\mathrm{n}} = \sum_{\mathrm{i}} \big(\sum_{\mathrm{j}} \sigma_{\mathrm{ij}}\,n_{\mathrm{j}}\big)\,n_{\mathrm{i}}\), and exactly this double sum is the product of the row \(\vek n^\T\), the matrix \(\ten\sigma\) and the column \(\vek n\) ((1.41)). By item 3 of lemma 2.14 on splitting a vector, the shear stress is given by \(\tau^2 = |\vek t|^2 - \sigma_{\mathrm{n}}^2\). Together:

\[\sigma_{\mathrm{n}} = \vek n^\T\ten\sigma\,\vek n = \sum_{\mathrm{i}} \sum_{\mathrm{j}} n_{\mathrm{i}}\,\sigma_{\mathrm{ij}}\,n_{\mathrm{j}} , \qquad \tau^2 = |\ten\sigma\,\vek n|^2 - \sigma_{\mathrm{n}}^2 . \tag{2.43}\]

The double sum has nine terms. The terms \(n_{\mathrm{x}}\,\sigma_{\mathrm{xy}}\,n_{\mathrm{y}}\) and \(n_{\mathrm{y}}\,\sigma_{\mathrm{yx}}\,n_{\mathrm{x}}\) are equal because of the symmetry, and the same holds for the other two pairs, so written out

\[\sigma_{\mathrm{n}} = \sigma_{\mathrm{xx}}\,n_{\mathrm{x}}^2 + \sigma_{\mathrm{yy}}\,n_{\mathrm{y}}^2 + \sigma_{\mathrm{zz}}\,n_{\mathrm{z}}^2 + 2\,\sigma_{\mathrm{xy}}\,n_{\mathrm{x}} n_{\mathrm{y}} + 2\,\sigma_{\mathrm{xz}}\,n_{\mathrm{x}} n_{\mathrm{z}} + 2\,\sigma_{\mathrm{yz}}\,n_{\mathrm{y}} n_{\mathrm{z}} .\]

This is how CM (4.2.17) writes the normal stress and CM (4.2.18) the shear stress (PDF p. 184).

The formula for \(\sigma_{\mathrm{n}}\) has the same form as the strain of a fibre in the direction \(\vek n\) in (1.53), only with \(\sigma_{\mathrm{ij}}\) instead of \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{ij}}\). The reason is that both quantities are built in the same way: a matrix maps the direction \(\vek n\) to a vector, and we project this vector back onto the direction \(\vek n\). For stress this vector is the force per unit area \(\ten\sigma\vek n\). For strain it is \(\mat H\vek n\), approximately the difference of the displacements of the ends of a short fibre in the direction \(\vek n\), divided by its length (section 1.17). Its projection onto the direction of the fibre is \(\vek n^\T\mat H\vek n = \vek n^\T\ten\varepsilon\,\vek n\), because in the double sum the terms \(n_{\mathrm{i}}\,H_{\mathrm{ij}}\,n_{\mathrm{j}}\) and \(n_{\mathrm{j}}\,H_{\mathrm{ji}}\,n_{\mathrm{i}}\) combine into \(2\,n_{\mathrm{i}}\,\varepsilon_{\mathrm{ij}}\,n_{\mathrm{j}}\).

Let us test the formulas on the pure shear of section 2.6.6. The cube is loaded only by forces along its faces. The axis \(x\) points to the right, the axis \(z\) up, we pull the top face to the right, the bottom one to the left, the right one up and the left one down, all with the same force per unit area \(\tau_0 = 50\) MPa. The only nonzero stress components are \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xz}} = \sigma_{\mathrm{zx}} = \tau_0\). Take the face with the normal \(\vek n = (\tfrac35, 0, \tfrac45)\), which is perpendicular to neither diagonal of the cube (figure 2.50). By (2.42),

\[\vek t(\vek n) = \ten\sigma\,\vek n = \begin{bmatrix} 0 & 0 & \tau_0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 \\ \tau_0 & 0 & 0 \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} 3/5 \\ 0 \\ 4/5 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} \tfrac45\,\tau_0 \\ 0 \\ \tfrac35\,\tau_0 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 40 \\ 0 \\ 30 \end{bmatrix} \text{MPa} .\]

By (2.43) the normal stress is \(\sigma_{\mathrm{n}} = 2\,\sigma_{\mathrm{xz}}\,n_{\mathrm{x}} n_{\mathrm{z}} = 2 \cdot 50 \cdot \tfrac35 \cdot \tfrac45 = 48\) MPa, which is also \(\vek t\cdot\vek n = 40 \cdot \tfrac35 + 30 \cdot \tfrac45 = 24 + 24 = 48\) MPa. The traction vector has the size \(|\vek t| = \sqrt{40^2 + 30^2} = 50\) MPa, and the shear stress is \(\tau = \sqrt{50^2 - 48^2} = \sqrt{196} = 14\) MPa. The shear part is \(\vek t - \sigma_{\mathrm{n}}\vek n = 14\ \text{MPa} \cdot (\tfrac45, 0, -\tfrac35)\), and it is indeed perpendicular to \(\vek n\), since \(\tfrac45 \cdot \tfrac35 + 0 \cdot 0 - \tfrac35 \cdot \tfrac45 = 0\). On the face perpendicular to the diagonal \(AC\), with the normal \(\tfrac{1}{\sqrt2}(1, 0, 1)\), the normal stress was \(50\) MPa and there was no shear stress (section 2.6.6). The normal of our face is close to that normal, so the normal stress is close to \(50\) MPa and the shear stress is small.

2.9.3 Stress in turned axes

Now we can answer the first question from the beginning of the section. The component \(\bar\sigma_{\mathrm{kl}}\) in the new axes is the component \(l\) of the traction vector on the face perpendicular to the new axis \(k\). We know this vector from Cauchy's formula in the old axes, and its component along the new axis \(l\) we get by lemma 2.38 as the projection onto \(\bar{\vek e}_{\mathrm{l}}\). The indices \(i\), \(j\), \(k\) and \(l\) run over \(x\), \(y\) and \(z\). The first two count the old axes, the other two the new ones.

Theorem 2.42 Transformation of stress components (transformacija komponent napetosti)

Let \(P\) be a point of a body at which Cauchy's formula holds (theorem 2.24), \(\ten\sigma\) the stress matrix at \(P\) in the old rectangular Cartesian coordinate system, \(\bar{\ten\sigma}\) the stress matrix at \(P\) in the new system with the same unit of length, and \(\mat Q\) the rotation matrix from the old system to the new one. Then

\[\bar\sigma_{\mathrm{kl}} = \sum_{\mathrm{i}} \sum_{\mathrm{j}} Q_{\mathrm{ki}}\,\sigma_{\mathrm{ij}}\,Q_{\mathrm{lj}} , \qquad \bar{\ten\sigma} = \mat Q\,\ten\sigma\,\mat Q^\T . \tag{2.44}\]
Proof

We must show that the component \(l\) of the traction vector on the face with the normal \(\bar{\vek e}_{\mathrm{k}}\), written in the new system, equals the double sum.

  1. By definition 2.25 of the stress components, applied in the new system, \(\bar\sigma_{\mathrm{kl}}\) is the component \(l\) of the vector \(\vek t(\bar{\vek e}_{\mathrm{k}})\) in the new system. By item 1 of lemma 2.38 on the components of a vector in turned axes this is \(\bar\sigma_{\mathrm{kl}} = \vek t(\bar{\vek e}_{\mathrm{k}})\cdot\bar{\vek e}_{\mathrm{l}}\).
  2. The vector \(\vek t(\bar{\vek e}_{\mathrm{k}})\) is determined by the force on a patch and its area, not by the choice of axes (definition 2.20), so we may compute it in the old system. Cauchy's formula holds in every rectangular Cartesian coordinate system, so also in the old one. We apply it to the normal \(\bar{\vek e}_{\mathrm{k}}\), which has the components \(Q_{\mathrm{kx}}\), \(Q_{\mathrm{ky}}\), \(Q_{\mathrm{kz}}\) in the old system (definition 2.37). By (2.22), \(\vek t(\bar{\vek e}_{\mathrm{k}}) = \sum_{\mathrm{i}} Q_{\mathrm{ki}}\,\vek t(\vek e_{\mathrm{i}})\).
  3. We substitute into step 1 and by items 2 and 3 of the properties of the scalar product (lemma 2.12) take out the numbers: \(\bar\sigma_{\mathrm{kl}} = \sum_{\mathrm{i}} Q_{\mathrm{ki}}\,\big(\vek t(\vek e_{\mathrm{i}})\cdot\bar{\vek e}_{\mathrm{l}}\big)\).
  4. We compute the scalar product in the brackets with the components in the old system. By (2.23), \(\vek t(\vek e_{\mathrm{i}}) = (\sigma_{\mathrm{ix}}, \sigma_{\mathrm{iy}}, \sigma_{\mathrm{iz}})\), by the definition of the rotation matrix \(\bar{\vek e}_{\mathrm{l}} = (Q_{\mathrm{lx}}, Q_{\mathrm{ly}}, Q_{\mathrm{lz}})\), and by (2.6) \(\vek t(\vek e_{\mathrm{i}})\cdot\bar{\vek e}_{\mathrm{l}} = \sum_{\mathrm{j}} \sigma_{\mathrm{ij}}\,Q_{\mathrm{lj}}\).
  5. We substitute step 4 into step 3 and get \(\bar\sigma_{\mathrm{kl}} = \sum_{\mathrm{i}} \sum_{\mathrm{j}} Q_{\mathrm{ki}}\,\sigma_{\mathrm{ij}}\,Q_{\mathrm{lj}}\).
  6. By definitions 1.100 and 1.98 the inner sum \(\sum_{\mathrm{j}} \sigma_{\mathrm{ij}}\,Q_{\mathrm{lj}} = \sum_{\mathrm{j}} \sigma_{\mathrm{ij}}\,(\mat Q^\T)_{\mathrm{jl}}\) is the entry in row \(i\) and column \(l\) of the product \(\ten\sigma\,\mat Q^\T\). The outer sum \(\sum_{\mathrm{i}} Q_{\mathrm{ki}}\,(\ten\sigma\,\mat Q^\T)_{\mathrm{il}}\) is the entry in row \(k\) and column \(l\) of the product \(\mat Q\,(\ten\sigma\,\mat Q^\T)\). We do not write the brackets, because the matrix product is associative (item 2 of lemma 1.99 on the properties of the matrix product).

Source: CM (4.3.3) (PDF p. 186), SADD (3.3.1) (PDF p. 68). CM has the transposed stress matrix, but since \((\mat Q\,\ten\sigma^\T\mat Q^\T)^\T = \mat Q\,\ten\sigma\,\mat Q^\T\), the rule has the same form in both conventions. The proof from Cauchy's formula is not from the sources.

The theorem says that for the components in the new axes we need no new reasoning about forces. The nine old components and the rotation matrix are enough, and every new component is a sum of nine products. The theorem needs no approximation and no property of the material, so it holds wherever Cauchy's formula holds. It also matters what the proof did not use: the symmetry of the stress components. So the rule also holds for a matrix that is not symmetric. When \(\ten\sigma\) is symmetric, \(\bar{\ten\sigma}\) is symmetric too. By lemma 1.101 on the transposed product, \(\bar{\ten\sigma}^\T = (\mat Q^\T)^\T\,\ten\sigma^\T\mat Q^\T = \mat Q\,\ten\sigma\,\mat Q^\T = \bar{\ten\sigma}\). This is as it must be, since the second condition of equilibrium, and with it the theorem on the symmetry of stress, holds in every right-handed coordinate system. For a mirrored system, for which we did not prove the theorem, this very computation gives the symmetry. The way back we get by multiplying both sides of (2.44) by \(\mat Q^\T\) from the left and by \(\mat Q\) from the right. Since \(\mat Q^\T\mat Q = \mat I\) by (2.40), what remains is \(\ten\sigma = \mat Q^\T\bar{\ten\sigma}\,\mat Q\).

Most often we turn the axes about one of them. For the turn about the axis \(z\), the row \(x\) of the matrix \(\mat Q\) has the entries \(c\), \(s\), \(0\), and the row \(y\) the entries \(-s\), \(c\), \(0\). Let us compute \(\bar\sigma_{\mathrm{xx}}\) by (2.44).

  1. For \(k = l = x\), \(\bar\sigma_{\mathrm{xx}} = \sum_{\mathrm{i}} \sum_{\mathrm{j}} Q_{\mathrm{xi}}\,\sigma_{\mathrm{ij}}\,Q_{\mathrm{xj}}\). Since \(Q_{\mathrm{xz}} = 0\), only the terms in which \(i\) and \(j\) are \(x\) or \(y\) differ from zero:
    \[\bar\sigma_{\mathrm{xx}} = Q_{\mathrm{xx}}\,\sigma_{\mathrm{xx}}\,Q_{\mathrm{xx}} + Q_{\mathrm{xx}}\,\sigma_{\mathrm{xy}}\,Q_{\mathrm{xy}} + Q_{\mathrm{xy}}\,\sigma_{\mathrm{yx}}\,Q_{\mathrm{xx}} + Q_{\mathrm{xy}}\,\sigma_{\mathrm{yy}}\,Q_{\mathrm{xy}} .\]
  2. We substitute \(Q_{\mathrm{xx}} = c\) and \(Q_{\mathrm{xy}} = s\): \(\bar\sigma_{\mathrm{xx}} = c^2\,\sigma_{\mathrm{xx}} + cs\,\sigma_{\mathrm{xy}} + sc\,\sigma_{\mathrm{yx}} + s^2\,\sigma_{\mathrm{yy}}\).
  3. By the theorem on the symmetry of stress, \(\sigma_{\mathrm{yx}} = \sigma_{\mathrm{xy}}\), so the two middle terms combine into \(2cs\,\sigma_{\mathrm{xy}}\).

In the same way we get the other components. We checked all of them with SymPy:

\[\begin{aligned} \bar\sigma_{\mathrm{xx}} &= c^2\,\sigma_{\mathrm{xx}} + s^2\,\sigma_{\mathrm{yy}} + 2cs\,\sigma_{\mathrm{xy}} , \\ \bar\sigma_{\mathrm{yy}} &= s^2\,\sigma_{\mathrm{xx}} + c^2\,\sigma_{\mathrm{yy}} - 2cs\,\sigma_{\mathrm{xy}} , \\ \bar\sigma_{\mathrm{xy}} &= -cs\,\sigma_{\mathrm{xx}} + cs\,\sigma_{\mathrm{yy}} + (c^2 - s^2)\,\sigma_{\mathrm{xy}} , \\ \bar\sigma_{\mathrm{xz}} &= c\,\sigma_{\mathrm{xz}} + s\,\sigma_{\mathrm{yz}} , \qquad \bar\sigma_{\mathrm{yz}} = -s\,\sigma_{\mathrm{xz}} + c\,\sigma_{\mathrm{yz}} , \qquad \bar\sigma_{\mathrm{zz}} = \sigma_{\mathrm{zz}} . \end{aligned} \tag{2.45}\]

With \(c = \cos\theta\) and \(s = \sin\theta\) the first three lines are the formulas SADD (3.3.4) (PDF p. 68), and all of them are also written in CM (4.3.7) (PDF p. 187), where \(2cs\) and \(c^2 - s^2\) are expressed with the double angle.

Let us test the rule on the bar of section 2.2. This is a steel bar with a diameter of 10 mm, pulled at both ends by a force of 10 kN, with the axis \(x\) along the bar, the axis \(y\) up and the axis \(z\) toward us. Far from the ends the only nonzero stress component is \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xx}} = \sigma = 127{,}32\) MPa (section 2.6.6). We turn the axes about the axis \(z\) with \(c = 0{,}6\) and \(s = 0{,}8\), so with \(c^2 = 0{,}36\), \(s^2 = 0{,}64\) and \(cs = 0{,}48\). By (2.45),

\[\begin{aligned} \bar\sigma_{\mathrm{xx}} &= 0{,}36\,\sigma = 45{,}84\ \text{MPa} , \\ \bar\sigma_{\mathrm{yy}} &= 0{,}64\,\sigma = 81{,}49\ \text{MPa} , \\ \bar\sigma_{\mathrm{xy}} &= -0{,}48\,\sigma = -61{,}12\ \text{MPa} , \end{aligned}\]

and all other components are zero (figure 2.51). Does this agree with section 2.4? The face with the normal \(\bar{\vek e}_{\mathrm{x}} = (\tfrac35, \tfrac45, 0)\) is the oblique cut with \(\cos\theta = 0{,}6\). By (2.13) the normal stress on it is \(\sigma\cos^2\theta = 0{,}36\,\sigma\), and by (2.14) the shear stress is \(\sigma\sin\theta\cos\theta = 0{,}48\,\sigma\). There we also computed that the shear part equals \(-\sigma\sin\theta\cos\theta\,\vek d\), where \(\vek d = (-\sin\theta, \cos\theta, 0)\) is exactly \(\bar{\vek e}_{\mathrm{y}}\). So its component along the axis \(\bar y\) is \(-0{,}48\,\sigma\), which is \(\bar\sigma_{\mathrm{xy}}\). Besides the size of the shear stress the rule also gives its direction: the shear part points opposite to the axis \(\bar y\).

The numbers hold one more pattern: \(\bar\sigma_{\mathrm{xx}} + \bar\sigma_{\mathrm{yy}} = 0{,}36\,\sigma + 0{,}64\,\sigma = \sigma\). The normal stresses on two perpendicular faces add up to \(\sigma\), as we saw in the table of section 2.4 at \(30^\circ\) and \(60^\circ\). The first two lines of (2.45) tell why. When we add them, the terms \(2cs\,\sigma_{\mathrm{xy}}\) and \(-2cs\,\sigma_{\mathrm{xy}}\) cancel, and what remains is \((c^2 + s^2)\,(\sigma_{\mathrm{xx}} + \sigma_{\mathrm{yy}}) = \sigma_{\mathrm{xx}} + \sigma_{\mathrm{yy}}\). So in a turn about the axis \(z\) the sum \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xx}} + \sigma_{\mathrm{yy}}\) does not change. That in every turn the sum of all three diagonal components does not change we will show in section 2.11.

The second example is the pure shear of section 2.9.2: the cube is loaded only by forces along its faces, of size \(\tau_0\) per unit area, and the only nonzero stress components are \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xz}} = \sigma_{\mathrm{zx}} = \tau_0\). In section 2.6.6 we found with Cauchy's formula, face by face, that there is no shear on the faces perpendicular to the diagonals of the cube. Now we place the axes along the diagonals and compute all nine components at once. We look at the cube from the front as in figure 2.28, with the corners \(A\) bottom left, \(B\) bottom right, \(C\) top right and \(D\) top left. Let the new axis \(\bar x\) point along the diagonal from \(A\) toward \(C\), the new axis \(\bar z\) along the diagonal from \(B\) toward \(D\), and let the axis \(\bar y\) stay the axis \(y\):

\[\bar{\vek e}_{\mathrm{x}} = \tfrac{1}{\sqrt2}\,(1, 0, 1) , \qquad \bar{\vek e}_{\mathrm{y}} = (0, 1, 0) , \qquad \bar{\vek e}_{\mathrm{z}} = \tfrac{1}{\sqrt2}\,(-1, 0, 1) .\]

All three are unit vectors, for example \(|\bar{\vek e}_{\mathrm{x}}|^2 = \tfrac12\,(1 + 0 + 1) = 1\), and pairwise perpendicular, for example \(\bar{\vek e}_{\mathrm{x}}\cdot\bar{\vek e}_{\mathrm{z}} = \tfrac12\,(-1 + 0 + 1) = 0\). This is a turn about the axis \(y\) by an eighth of a full turn. We compute the product of three matrices in two steps.

  1. By definition 1.98 the entry \((i, l)\) of the product \(\ten\sigma\,\mat Q^\T\) is \(\sum_{\mathrm{j}} \sigma_{\mathrm{ij}}\,Q_{\mathrm{lj}}\), that is, the scalar product of the row \(i\) of the matrix \(\ten\sigma\) with the row \(l\) of the matrix \(\mat Q\), the vector \(\bar{\vek e}_{\mathrm{l}}\). The row \(x\) of the matrix \(\ten\sigma\) has the entries \(0\), \(0\), \(\tau_0\), and its scalar products with \(\bar{\vek e}_{\mathrm{x}}\), \(\bar{\vek e}_{\mathrm{y}}\), \(\bar{\vek e}_{\mathrm{z}}\) are \(\tau_0/\sqrt2\), \(0\), \(\tau_0/\sqrt2\). The row \(y\) is zero. The row \(z\) has the entries \(\tau_0\), \(0\), \(0\), and its scalar products are \(\tau_0/\sqrt2\), \(0\), \(-\tau_0/\sqrt2\). So
    \[\ten\sigma\,\mat Q^\T = \frac{\tau_0}{\sqrt2} \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 & 1 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 \\ 1 & 0 & -1 \end{bmatrix} .\]
  2. The entry \((k, l)\) of the product \(\mat Q\,(\ten\sigma\,\mat Q^\T)\) is the sum of the products of corresponding entries of the row \(k\) of the matrix \(\mat Q\) and the column \(l\) of the matrix above. The row \(x\) of the matrix \(\mat Q\) has the entries \(\tfrac{1}{\sqrt2}\), \(0\), \(\tfrac{1}{\sqrt2}\). With the column \(x\) of the matrix above, with the entries \(\tfrac{\tau_0}{\sqrt2}\), \(0\), \(\tfrac{\tau_0}{\sqrt2}\), it gives \(\bar\sigma_{\mathrm{xx}} = \tfrac{\tau_0}{2}\,(1 + 1) = \tau_0\), and with the column \(z\), with the entries \(\tfrac{\tau_0}{\sqrt2}\), \(0\), \(-\tfrac{\tau_0}{\sqrt2}\), it gives \(\bar\sigma_{\mathrm{xz}} = \tfrac{\tau_0}{2}\,(1 - 1) = 0\). The row \(z\) of the matrix \(\mat Q\) has the entries \(-\tfrac{1}{\sqrt2}\), \(0\), \(\tfrac{1}{\sqrt2}\) and gives with the column \(x\) the number \(\bar\sigma_{\mathrm{zx}} = \tfrac{\tau_0}{2}\,(-1 + 1) = 0\) and with the column \(z\) the number \(\bar\sigma_{\mathrm{zz}} = \tfrac{\tau_0}{2}\,(-1 - 1) = -\tau_0\). The row \(y\) of the matrix \(\mat Q\) has the entries \(0\), \(1\), \(0\) and picks out the row \(y\) of the matrix above, which is zero. So
    \[\bar{\ten\sigma} = \begin{bmatrix} \tau_0 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & -\tau_0 \end{bmatrix} .\]

In the axes along the diagonals the same stress has no shear component at all. On the faces perpendicular to the diagonal \(AC\) the tension \(\tau_0\) acts, and on the faces perpendicular to the diagonal \(BD\) the compression \(\tau_0\) (figure 2.52). This is what we found in section 2.6.6 with Cauchy's formula for each face separately, now in one computation for all faces perpendicular to the new axes. For \(\tau_0 = 50\) MPa, \(\bar\sigma_{\mathrm{xx}} = 50\) MPa and \(\bar\sigma_{\mathrm{zz}} = -50\) MPa. The sum of the diagonal components is zero before the turn and after it.

2.9.4 Strain in turned axes

Do the strain components also change by the same rule? In section 1.17 we got the components of the small strain tensor from the partial derivatives of the displacement field, \(\ten\varepsilon = \tfrac12\,(\mat H + \mat H^\T)\) ((1.51)), where \(\mat H\) is the displacement gradient at the point \(P\) with the entries \(H_{\mathrm{ij}} = \partial u_{\mathrm{i}}/\partial x_{\mathrm{j}}\) (definition 1.109). Here \(x_{\mathrm{j}}\) means the coordinate \(x\), \(y\) or \(z\). In the new axes the displacement has the components \(\bar u_{\mathrm{k}}\), which by lemma 2.38 we get from the old ones, and the points have the new coordinates \(\bar x_{\mathrm{l}}\).
