CM finds the largest value with Lagrange multipliers, which the book does not have yet, and states the solutions of the resulting equations without derivation (PDF p. 191).

The proof showed why the theorem holds. In step 4 we saw that the average of the squares of the distances from any point \(c\) equals the average of the squares of the distances from the balance point \(\sigma_{\mathrm{n}}\), increased by \((\sigma_{\mathrm{n}} - c)^2\). The balance point is therefore the point of least spread. Around the midpoint of the interval \([\sigma_3, \sigma_1]\), however, the weights are spread by at most half the length of the interval. We will use the expression (2.67) with weights again for the faces that are equally inclined to all three principal directions.

Figure 2.77 shows on which faces the shear is largest. The normal \((\vek e_1 + \vek e_3)/\sqrt2\) lies halfway between the principal directions \(\vek e_1\) and \(\vek e_3\) and is perpendicular to \(\vek e_2\). The face therefore contains the principal direction \(\vek e_2\) and lies halfway between the faces perpendicular to \(\vek e_1\) and \(\vek e_3\). There are two faces with the largest shear, and they are perpendicular to each other, because \((\vek e_1 + \vek e_3)\cdot(\vek e_1 - \vek e_3) = 1 - 1 = 0\). The normal stress on them is in general not zero but \((\sigma_1 + \sigma_3)/2\). The intermediate principal stress \(\sigma_2\) does not appear in \(\tau_{\max}\). If all three principal stresses are different, there are no other faces with the largest shear. Equality in step 8 of the proof requires \(w_2 = 0\), because \(\sigma_2\) is less than half the length away from \(c\), and equality in step 5 requires \(\sigma_{\mathrm{n}} = c\), which together with \(w_1 + w_3 = 1\) gives \(w_1 = w_3 = \tfrac12\).

Let us test the theorem on the examples.

The bar. In a bar pulled by an axial force with the stress \(\sigma > 0\) in the cross section, the principal stresses are \(\sigma_1 = \sigma\) and \(\sigma_2 = \sigma_3 = 0\). The theorem gives \(\tau_{\max} = \sigma/2\), so for our bar with diameter 10 mm under the force 10 kN, \(127{,}3/2 = 63{,}7\) MPa. This is the value of lemma 2.19 on the largest shear stress in a bar, except that we now know it is the largest among all faces through the point, not only among the faces tilted about the axis \(z\). Since \(\sigma_2\) and \(\sigma_3\) are equal, there are many faces with the largest shear. Every normal with \(n_1^2 = \tfrac12\) gives the weights \(w_1 = \tfrac12\) and \(w_2 + w_3 = \tfrac12\), and how the second half is shared between \(\sigma_2 = 0\) and \(\sigma_3 = 0\) does not matter, because both sit at the same point of the line. All such faces are tilted by \(45^\circ\) from the cross section, in any direction around the axis of the bar. For a bar that is compressed, \(\sigma < 0\), the principal stresses are \(\sigma_1 = \sigma_2 = 0\) and \(\sigma_3 = \sigma\), and the theorem gives \(\tau_{\max} = (0 - \sigma)/2 = |\sigma|/2\), again as in the lemma.

Pure shear. The cube of section 2.6.6 is loaded only by forces along four of its faces, \(\tau_0\) per unit area (figure 2.28). In it \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xz}} = \sigma_{\mathrm{zx}} = \tau_0\) and the other components are zero, so the principal stresses are \(\tau_0\) along the diagonal \(AC\), \(0\) along the axis \(y\) and \(-\tau_0\) along the diagonal \(BD\) (section 2.11). Hence \(\vek e_1 = (1, 0, 1)/\sqrt2\), \(\vek e_2 = (0, 1, 0)\) and \(\vek e_3 = (-1, 0, 1)/\sqrt2\), and the theorem gives \(\tau_{\max} = (\tau_0 - (-\tau_0))/2 = \tau_0\). The two faces with the largest shear have the normals

\[\frac{\vek e_1 + \vek e_3}{\sqrt2} = \frac{(0, 0, 2)}{2} = \vek e_{\mathrm{z}} , \qquad \frac{\vek e_1 - \vek e_3}{\sqrt2} = \frac{(2, 0, 0)}{2} = \vek e_{\mathrm{x}} .\]

These are just the faces of the cube, on which the shear force \(\tau_0\) per unit area acts, and the normal stress on them is \((\tau_0 + (-\tau_0))/2 = 0\), as it must be. On no other face through a point of the cube is the shear larger than \(\tau_0\).

The fluid at rest. All three principal stresses are \(-p\), and \(\tau_{\max} = 0\): there is no shear stress on any face.

A thin plate. Now we need an example in which all three principal stresses are different. Take a thin steel plate lying in the plane of the axes \(x\) and \(y\), with edges parallel to the axes (figure 2.78). On its edges act forces parallel to the plane of the plate and spread evenly along the edge. Per unit area the force on the right edge, whose outward normal is \(\vek e_{\mathrm{x}}\), is \((90, 40, 0)\) MPa, on the top edge with outward normal \(\vek e_{\mathrm{y}}\) it is \((40, 30, 0)\) MPa, and on the opposite edges the opposite forces act. The faces of the plate perpendicular to the axis \(z\) are not loaded. We neglect the weight of the plate. As for the bar and for pure shear, we assume that the stress is the same at all points of the plate. Then the traction vector on the face with normal \(\vek e_{\mathrm{x}}\) at every point of the plate equals the force per unit area on the right edge, \(\vek t(\vek e_{\mathrm{x}}) = (90, 40, 0)\) MPa, and likewise \(\vek t(\vek e_{\mathrm{y}}) = (40, 30, 0)\) MPa. By definition 2.25, therefore, \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xx}} = 90\) MPa, \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xy}} = 40\) MPa, \(\sigma_{\mathrm{yx}} = 40\) MPa and \(\sigma_{\mathrm{yy}} = 30\) MPa. Since the faces of the plate are not loaded, \(\vek t(\vek e_{\mathrm{z}}) = \vek 0\) on them, and since the stress is the same everywhere, \(\sigma_{\mathrm{zx}} = \sigma_{\mathrm{zy}} = \sigma_{\mathrm{zz}} = 0\) in the whole plate. By the symmetry of stress, \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xz}}\) and \(\sigma_{\mathrm{yz}}\) are zero too. Such a state, in which the components with the index \(z\) are zero, is called plane stress (ravninsko napetostno stanje). For a thin plate loaded only in its plane it is a good approximation even when the stress is not the same everywhere, because the components with the index \(z\) cannot change much from the unloaded faces to the middle of the thickness (SADD §7.2, PDF p. 152). We chose the numbers so that the computations stay transparent and the steel does not yield, as we will check in section 2.12.5.

We get the principal stresses of the plate from the characteristic equation (lemma 2.64). The stress matrix is

\[\ten\sigma = \begin{pmatrix} 90 & 40 & 0 \\ 40 & 30 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 \end{pmatrix}\ \text{MPa} .\]

In the six-term formula for the determinant (2.51) of the matrix \(\ten\sigma - \lambda\mat I\) every term contains one entry from each row. In the third row only the entry \(-\lambda\) is nonzero, so only the two terms that contain it remain (we leave out MPa):

\[\begin{aligned} \det(\ten\sigma - \lambda\mat I) &= -\lambda\,\big((90 - \lambda)(30 - \lambda) - 40 \cdot 40\big) \\ &= -\lambda\,(\lambda^2 - 120\,\lambda + 1100) = -\lambda\,(\lambda - 110)(\lambda - 10) . \end{aligned}\]

We check the last equality by multiplying out: \((\lambda - 110)(\lambda - 10) = \lambda^2 - 120\,\lambda + 1100\). The principal stresses are therefore \(\sigma_1 = 110\) MPa, \(\sigma_2 = 10\) MPa and \(\sigma_3 = 0\). We check the principal directions by multiplication:

\[\begin{aligned} \ten\sigma\,(2, 1, 0) &= (220, 110, 0) = 110\,(2, 1, 0) , \\ \ten\sigma\,(-1, 2, 0) &= (-10, 20, 0) = 10\,(-1, 2, 0) , \\ \ten\sigma\,(0, 0, 1) &= \vek 0 . \end{aligned}\]

The vectors \((2, 1, 0)\) and \((-1, 2, 0)\) have length \(\sqrt5\), so the unit vectors of the principal directions are \(\vek e_1 = (2, 1, 0)/\sqrt5\), \(\vek e_2 = (-1, 2, 0)/\sqrt5\) and \(\vek e_3 = \vek e_{\mathrm{z}}\).

Theorem 2.70 gives \(\tau_{\max} = (110 - 0)/2 = 55\) MPa on the faces with the normals

\[\frac{\vek e_1 \pm \vek e_3}{\sqrt2} = \frac{(2, 1, \pm\sqrt5)}{\sqrt{10}} .\]

We check this directly for the plus sign. By Cauchy's formula \(\vek t = \ten\sigma\,\vek n = (220, 110, 0)/\sqrt{10}\), the normal stress is \(\sigma_{\mathrm{n}} = \vek t\cdot\vek n = (440 + 110)/10 = 55\) MPa, \(|\vek t|^2 = (48\,400 + 12\,100)/10 = 6050\) MPa², and \(\tau^2 = 6050 - 55^2 = 3025\) MPa², so \(\tau = 55\) MPa. As an additional test we computed with NumPy the shear stress on 200 000 randomly chosen faces. The largest was \(54{,}9996\) MPa, none exceeded 55 MPa. These two faces are not perpendicular to the plate, because their normals have a \(z\) component. They cut the plate obliquely, through its thickness. Someone who looked only at the faces perpendicular to the plate would not find the largest shear, as we will see in the next section.

2.12.3 Mohr's circle

The theorem says how large the largest shear is, but not how the normal and the shear stress change as we turn the face. For the bar we showed this with the graph in figure 2.20, with one curve for each stress. A nicer picture results if we draw each face as one point in a plane, with the normal stress on the horizontal axis and the shear stress on the vertical one. For faces that turn about one principal direction, these points lie on a circle.

The stress at a point was shown in the mathematical theory of elasticity by a surface drawn by Cauchy (section 2.11), which TIMO calls the ellipsoid of stress, and in plane problems by an ellipse (TIMO, PDF p. 117 and 224). Culmann showed in his book Graphische Statik in 1866 that the stress in a plane system can be represented by a circle, which simplifies the problem greatly (TIMO, PDF p. 224). The normal and the shear stress on each face are the coordinates of one point on a circle whose diameter is the difference of the two principal stresses (TIMO, PDF p. 224 and 225). Mohr did the same for three principal stresses and got three circles. The largest has as its diameter the difference of the largest and the smallest principal stress and belongs to the faces that contain the direction of the middle principal stress. The points of all other faces lie in the region between the circles (TIMO, PDF p. 225). We shall see the proof in lemma 2.72. For a given normal stress the shear is largest exactly on the faces that contain the direction of the middle principal stress (TIMO, PDF p. 225).

With this circle Mohr solved another problem too, strength. Most engineers of the time followed Saint-Venant and took the largest strain as the measure of failure. They determined the dimensions of parts so that the largest strain at the most endangered place under the most unfavourable loading does not exceed the permissible extension in simple tension (TIMO, PDF p. 226). Coulomb had already assumed that failure is triggered by shear (section 1.1, TIMO, PDF p. 226). In Munich, where the first laboratory for testing materials was founded in 1871, Johann Bauschinger determined with a sensitive gauge the stresses up to which steel returns to its original shape after unloading, in tension, compression and shear (TIMO, PDF p. 218, 219 and 226). These results did not agree with the measure of the largest strain (TIMO, PDF p. 226). In a paper of 1882 Mohr treated Bauschinger's experiments and with circles designed a measure that can be adapted to different states of stress and better matched to experiments (TIMO, PDF p. 226). He assumed that among the faces with the same normal stress the one with the largest shear fails first, that is the one on the largest circle, so only the largest circle matters (TIMO, PDF p. 226). He drew such a circle for every test in which the material failed, and drew through the circles an envelope, a line that touches all the circles. For a loading that was not tested, failure occurs when the largest circle touches the envelope (TIMO, PDF p. 226). For cast iron, that is iron poured into a mould (figure 2.79), he took as the envelope the two outer tangents of the circles of the tensile and the compressive test. The circle with its centre at the origin that touches the envelope gave the strength in shear, which agreed satisfactorily with experiments (TIMO, PDF p. 226 and 227).

To make the picture complete we need a sign for the shear stress. The shear stress \(\tau\) is a length and so never negative, while the direction of the shear part says in which direction along the face it acts. We consider faces with normal \(\vek n = (n_{\mathrm{x}}, n_{\mathrm{y}}, 0)\), where \(n_{\mathrm{x}}^2 + n_{\mathrm{y}}^2 = 1\). These faces contain the direction of the axis \(z\), like the cuts of the bar in section 2.4. In each such face we choose the direction

\[\vek d = (-n_{\mathrm{y}},\ n_{\mathrm{x}},\ 0) ,\]

which is perpendicular to \(\vek n\) and to \(\vek e_{\mathrm{z}}\), like the vector \(\vek d\) in section 2.4, where \(\vek n = (\cos\theta, \sin\theta, 0)\) and \(\vek d = (-\sin\theta, \cos\theta, 0)\). We define the shear component (strižna komponenta) along \(\vek d\) as the projection of the traction vector onto \(\vek d\),

\[\tau_{\mathrm{nd}} = \vek t(\vek n)\cdot\vek d .\]

We will need the condition \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xz}} = \sigma_{\mathrm{yz}} = 0\). Then by the symmetry of stress also \(\sigma_{\mathrm{zx}} = \sigma_{\mathrm{zy}} = 0\), the traction vector on the face with normal \(\vek e_{\mathrm{z}}\) is \(\vek t(\vek e_{\mathrm{z}}) = (0, 0, \sigma_{\mathrm{zz}})\) and points along the normal, so \(\vek e_{\mathrm{z}}\) is a principal direction. The faces that contain the direction of the axis \(z\) therefore turn about a principal direction. The next lemma says that the shear part of the traction vector is \(\tau_{\mathrm{nd}}\,\vek d\), so \(\tau = |\tau_{\mathrm{nd}}|\), and the sign tells whether the shear part points along \(\vek d\) or opposite to it.

Lemma 2.71 Mohr's circle (Mohrov krog)

Let the stress components at a point \(P\) be symmetric and let \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xz}} = \sigma_{\mathrm{yz}} = 0\). For a face through \(P\) with unit normal \(\vek n = (n_{\mathrm{x}}, n_{\mathrm{y}}, 0)\) let \(\vek d = (-n_{\mathrm{y}}, n_{\mathrm{x}}, 0)\), let \(\sigma_{\mathrm{n}}\) be the normal stress on it and \(\tau_{\mathrm{nd}} = \vek t(\vek n)\cdot\vek d\). Then:

  1. The shear part of the traction vector is \(\vek t(\vek n) - \sigma_{\mathrm{n}}\vek n = \tau_{\mathrm{nd}}\,\vek d\).
  2. The point \((\sigma_{\mathrm{n}}, \tau_{\mathrm{nd}})\) lies on the circle with centre \((m, 0)\) and radius \(R\):
    \[\begin{aligned} (\sigma_{\mathrm{n}} - m)^2 + \tau_{\mathrm{nd}}^2 &= R^2 , \\ m &= \frac{\sigma_{\mathrm{xx}} + \sigma_{\mathrm{yy}}}{2} , \\ R &= \sqrt{\Big(\frac{\sigma_{\mathrm{xx}} - \sigma_{\mathrm{yy}}}{2}\Big)^2 + \sigma_{\mathrm{xy}}^2} . \end{aligned} \tag{2.69}\]
  3. For every point \((\sigma, \tau)\) of this circle there is a normal \(\vek n = (n_{\mathrm{x}}, n_{\mathrm{y}}, 0)\) with \(\sigma_{\mathrm{n}} = \sigma\) and \(\tau_{\mathrm{nd}} = \tau\).
Proof

We derive all three items from Cauchy's formula and from \(n_{\mathrm{x}}^2 + n_{\mathrm{y}}^2 = 1\).

1. The shear part.

  1. By (2.24) with \(n_{\mathrm{z}} = 0\), \(\sigma_{\mathrm{yx}} = \sigma_{\mathrm{xy}}\) and \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xz}} = \sigma_{\mathrm{yz}} = 0\),
    \[\vek t(\vek n) = (\sigma_{\mathrm{xx}} n_{\mathrm{x}} + \sigma_{\mathrm{xy}} n_{\mathrm{y}},\ \ \sigma_{\mathrm{xy}} n_{\mathrm{x}} + \sigma_{\mathrm{yy}} n_{\mathrm{y}},\ \ 0) .\]
  2. The vector \(\vek d\) is a unit vector, because \(n_{\mathrm{y}}^2 + n_{\mathrm{x}}^2 = 1\), and perpendicular to \(\vek n\), because \(\vek d\cdot\vek n = -n_{\mathrm{y}} n_{\mathrm{x}} + n_{\mathrm{x}} n_{\mathrm{y}} = 0\).
  3. By item 1 of lemma 2.14 on splitting a vector, the shear part \(\vek v = \vek t(\vek n) - \sigma_{\mathrm{n}}\vek n\) is perpendicular to \(\vek n\), so \(v_{\mathrm{x}} n_{\mathrm{x}} + v_{\mathrm{y}} n_{\mathrm{y}} = 0\). Its \(z\) component is zero, because it is zero for \(\vek t(\vek n)\) and for \(\vek n\).
  4. We compute the vector \((\vek v\cdot\vek d)\,\vek d = (-v_{\mathrm{x}} n_{\mathrm{y}} + v_{\mathrm{y}} n_{\mathrm{x}})\,(-n_{\mathrm{y}}, n_{\mathrm{x}}, 0)\). Its \(x\) component is \(v_{\mathrm{x}} n_{\mathrm{y}}^2 - v_{\mathrm{y}} n_{\mathrm{y}} n_{\mathrm{x}}\). By step 3, \(v_{\mathrm{y}} n_{\mathrm{y}} = -v_{\mathrm{x}} n_{\mathrm{x}}\), so this is \(v_{\mathrm{x}} n_{\mathrm{y}}^2 + v_{\mathrm{x}} n_{\mathrm{x}}^2 = v_{\mathrm{x}}\). Likewise the \(y\) component is \(-v_{\mathrm{x}} n_{\mathrm{x}} n_{\mathrm{y}} + v_{\mathrm{y}} n_{\mathrm{x}}^2 = v_{\mathrm{y}} n_{\mathrm{y}}^2 + v_{\mathrm{y}} n_{\mathrm{x}}^2 = v_{\mathrm{y}}\). The \(z\) component is zero. Hence \(\vek v = (\vek v\cdot\vek d)\,\vek d\).
  5. By the rules of the scalar product, \(\vek v\cdot\vek d = \vek t(\vek n)\cdot\vek d - \sigma_{\mathrm{n}}\,(\vek n\cdot\vek d) = \tau_{\mathrm{nd}} - 0\). The shear part is therefore \(\tau_{\mathrm{nd}}\,\vek d\).

2. The circle.

  1. From step 1 and (2.6) we compute
    \[\begin{aligned} \sigma_{\mathrm{n}} &= \vek t(\vek n)\cdot\vek n = \sigma_{\mathrm{xx}} n_{\mathrm{x}}^2 + 2\sigma_{\mathrm{xy}} n_{\mathrm{x}} n_{\mathrm{y}} + \sigma_{\mathrm{yy}} n_{\mathrm{y}}^2 , \\ \tau_{\mathrm{nd}} &= \vek t(\vek n)\cdot\vek d = -\sigma_{\mathrm{xx}} n_{\mathrm{x}} n_{\mathrm{y}} + \sigma_{\mathrm{xy}}\,(n_{\mathrm{x}}^2 - n_{\mathrm{y}}^2) + \sigma_{\mathrm{yy}} n_{\mathrm{x}} n_{\mathrm{y}} . \end{aligned}\]
    These are the formulas for \(\bar\sigma_{\mathrm{xx}}\) and \(\bar\sigma_{\mathrm{xy}}\) of (2.45) with \(c = n_{\mathrm{x}}\) and \(s = n_{\mathrm{y}}\), since \(\vek n\) is the unit vector of the new axis \(\bar x\) and \(\vek d\) the unit vector of the new axis \(\bar y\).
  2. We introduce the auxiliary numbers \(C = n_{\mathrm{x}}^2 - n_{\mathrm{y}}^2\) and \(S = 2\,n_{\mathrm{x}} n_{\mathrm{y}}\). From \(n_{\mathrm{x}}^2 + n_{\mathrm{y}}^2 = 1\) it follows that \(n_{\mathrm{x}}^2 = (1 + C)/2\) and \(n_{\mathrm{y}}^2 = (1 - C)/2\), which we check by adding and subtracting the two equalities.
  3. We insert these into step 6 and write \(a = (\sigma_{\mathrm{xx}} - \sigma_{\mathrm{yy}})/2\) and \(b = \sigma_{\mathrm{xy}}\):
    \[\sigma_{\mathrm{n}} = \sigma_{\mathrm{xx}}\,\frac{1 + C}{2} + \sigma_{\mathrm{yy}}\,\frac{1 - C}{2} + \sigma_{\mathrm{xy}}\,S = m + a\,C + b\,S , \qquad \tau_{\mathrm{nd}} = -(\sigma_{\mathrm{xx}} - \sigma_{\mathrm{yy}})\,n_{\mathrm{x}} n_{\mathrm{y}} + \sigma_{\mathrm{xy}}\,C = b\,C - a\,S .\]
  4. We have \(C^2 + S^2 = (n_{\mathrm{x}}^2 - n_{\mathrm{y}}^2)^2 + 4n_{\mathrm{x}}^2 n_{\mathrm{y}}^2 = n_{\mathrm{x}}^4 + 2n_{\mathrm{x}}^2 n_{\mathrm{y}}^2 + n_{\mathrm{y}}^4 = (n_{\mathrm{x}}^2 + n_{\mathrm{y}}^2)^2 = 1\).
  5. When we write out the squares, the terms \(2abCS\) and \(-2abCS\) cancel:
    \[(\sigma_{\mathrm{n}} - m)^2 + \tau_{\mathrm{nd}}^2 = (aC + bS)^2 + (bC - aS)^2 = (a^2 + b^2)(C^2 + S^2) = a^2 + b^2 = R^2 .\]

3. Every point of the circle belongs to some face.

  1. If \(R = 0\), the circle is the single point \((m, 0)\), and by step 10 every normal gives it. Let \(R > 0\) and let the point \((\sigma, \tau)\) lie on the circle, \((\sigma - m)^2 + \tau^2 = R^2\). We set \(C = \big(a(\sigma - m) + b\tau\big)/R^2\) and \(S = \big(b(\sigma - m) - a\tau\big)/R^2\). Substituting, we check \(aC + bS = (a^2 + b^2)(\sigma - m)/R^2 = \sigma - m\) and \(bC - aS = (a^2 + b^2)\,\tau/R^2 = \tau\), and as in step 10, \(C^2 + S^2 = (a^2 + b^2)\big((\sigma - m)^2 + \tau^2\big)/R^4 = 1\).
  2. Hence \(-1 \le C \le 1\). We set \(n_{\mathrm{x}} = \sqrt{(1 + C)/2}\), and \(n_{\mathrm{y}} = \sqrt{(1 - C)/2}\) if \(S \ge 0\) and \(n_{\mathrm{y}} = -\sqrt{(1 - C)/2}\) if \(S < 0\). Then \(n_{\mathrm{x}}^2 + n_{\mathrm{y}}^2 = 1\), \(n_{\mathrm{x}}^2 - n_{\mathrm{y}}^2 = C\) and \(2n_{\mathrm{x}} n_{\mathrm{y}} = \pm\sqrt{1 - C^2} = \pm\sqrt{S^2} = S\), where the sign is that of \(S\).
  3. For this normal, by step 8, \(\sigma_{\mathrm{n}} = m + aC + bS = \sigma\) and \(\tau_{\mathrm{nd}} = bC - aS = \tau\).

Source: The formulas of step 8 are SADD (3.3.4), (3.3.5) (PDF p. 68) and BARBER (1.15), (1.16) (PDF p. 27), who calls them the equations of Mohr's circle. SADD derives Mohr's circles in space and names them after Otto Mohr (SADD (3.4.10), figure 3.7, PDF p. 71). The lemma in this form and the proof are not from the sources.

The lemma says that the points of all faces that contain the direction of the axis \(z\) lie on one circle, Mohr's circle (Mohrov krog). Its centre is on the horizontal axis, at the average of the normal stresses \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xx}}\) and \(\sigma_{\mathrm{yy}}\), and its radius depends on the difference of these stresses and on \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xy}}\). The face with normal \(\vek e_{\mathrm{x}}\) has \(\vek d = \vek e_{\mathrm{y}}\), its point is \((\sigma_{\mathrm{xx}}, \sigma_{\mathrm{xy}})\). The face with normal \(\vek e_{\mathrm{y}}\) has \(\vek d = -\vek e_{\mathrm{x}}\), its point is \((\sigma_{\mathrm{yy}}, -\sigma_{\mathrm{xy}})\). The midpoint of the segment between these two points is \((m, 0)\), the centre of the circle, so the two points are at the opposite ends of a diameter. Faces that are perpendicular in the body are opposite on the circle. From the circle we read off two things. The normal stress is largest and smallest at the points where the circle meets the horizontal axis, \(\sigma_{\mathrm{n}} = m \pm R\). There \(\tau_{\mathrm{nd}} = 0\), so these faces are principal and \(m \pm R\) are principal stresses. The shear stress is largest at the top and at the bottom of the circle, where \(|\tau_{\mathrm{nd}}| = R\) and \(\sigma_{\mathrm{n}} = m\).

Why are perpendicular faces opposite on the circle and not a quarter of the circle apart? Let us write the normal as in section 2.4, \(\vek n = (\cos\theta, \sin\theta, 0)\). Then the auxiliary numbers of the proof are

\[C = \cos^2\theta - \sin^2\theta = \cos 2\theta , \qquad S = 2\sin\theta\cos\theta = \sin 2\theta ,\]

by the double angle formulas for cosine and sine from school trigonometry (KREYSZIG Appendix A3.1, (7), PDF p. 1204). We also write the numbers \(a\) and \(b\) with an angle, \(a = R\cos\varphi\) and \(b = R\sin\varphi\), where \(\varphi\) is the angle between the horizontal axis and the radius to the point \((\sigma_{\mathrm{xx}}, \sigma_{\mathrm{xy}}) = (m + a, b)\). We may do this because \(a^2 + b^2 = R^2\). By step 8 of the proof and by the formulas for the cosine and sine of a difference of angles (KREYSZIG Appendix A3.1, (6), PDF p. 1204),

\[\begin{aligned} \sigma_{\mathrm{n}} - m &= R\,(\cos\varphi\cos 2\theta + \sin\varphi\sin 2\theta) = R\cos(\varphi - 2\theta) , \\ \tau_{\mathrm{nd}} &= R\,(\sin\varphi\cos 2\theta - \cos\varphi\sin 2\theta) = R\sin(\varphi - 2\theta) . \end{aligned}\]

When the normal turns by the angle \(\theta\) from the axis \(x\) toward the axis \(y\), the point on the circle turns by twice the angle, \(2\theta\), in the opposite sense. A face turned by a quarter turn is half the circle away, and a face turned by half a turn is the same face again, with normal \(-\vek n\), and the same point on the circle.

Let us test the circle on the bar pulled by an axial force. There \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xx}} = \sigma\) and all other components are zero. The condition of the lemma, \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xz}} = \sigma_{\mathrm{yz}} = 0\), holds, and \(m = \sigma/2\), \(R = \sqrt{(\sigma/2)^2 + 0} = \sigma/2\). The circle passes through the points \((0, 0)\) and \((\sigma, 0)\) (figure 2.80). By step 6 of the proof \(\tau_{\mathrm{nd}} = -\sigma\cos\theta\sin\theta\), which is the shear part \(-\sigma\sin\theta\cos\theta\,\vek d\) of step 4 in section 2.4. For the angle \(30^\circ\) the point is \((0{,}75\,\sigma,\ -0{,}433\,\sigma)\): the normal and the shear stress from the table in section 2.4, the shear one with a negative sign, because the shear part points opposite to \(\vek d\). Exactly, \(\tau_{\mathrm{nd}} = -\sigma\sin 30^\circ\cos 30^\circ = -\tfrac{\sqrt3}{4}\,\sigma\), and the point does lie on the circle: \((0{,}75 - 0{,}5)^2 + \tfrac{3}{16} = 0{,}0625 + 0{,}1875 = 0{,}25 = 0{,}5^2\). All five rows of the table are five points on the lower half of the circle. The faces with tilts between \(90^\circ\) and \(180^\circ\), which are the same as the faces with tilts between \(-90^\circ\) and \(0^\circ\), give the upper half.

Now the thin plate of figure 2.78, with the stresses \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xx}} = 90\) MPa, \(\sigma_{\mathrm{yy}} = 30\) MPa and \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xy}} = 40\) MPa, for the faces perpendicular to the plate. The condition of the lemma holds, because in plane stress \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xz}}\) and \(\sigma_{\mathrm{yz}}\) are zero. The centre of the circle is \(m = (90 + 30)/2 = 60\) MPa, the radius \(R = \sqrt{30^2 + 40^2} = 50\) MPa (figure 2.81). The face with normal \(\vek e_{\mathrm{x}}\) is the point \((90, 40)\), the face with normal \(\vek e_{\mathrm{y}}\) the point \((30, -40)\). The circle meets the horizontal axis at \(60 + 50 = 110\) MPa and at \(60 - 50 = 10\) MPa, which are the principal stresses \(\sigma_1\) and \(\sigma_2\) that we found above from the characteristic equation. Here \(a = 30 = 50 \cdot 0{,}6\) and \(b = 40 = 50 \cdot 0{,}8\), so \(\cos\varphi = 0{,}6\) and \(\sin\varphi = 0{,}8\). The principal face with \(\sigma_1\) is where \(\varphi - 2\theta = 0\), so \(\cos 2\theta = 0{,}6\) and \(\sin 2\theta = 0{,}8\). From \(C = n_{\mathrm{x}}^2 - n_{\mathrm{y}}^2 = 0{,}6\) and \(n_{\mathrm{x}}^2 + n_{\mathrm{y}}^2 = 1\) we get \(n_{\mathrm{x}}^2 = 0{,}8\) and \(n_{\mathrm{y}}^2 = 0{,}2\), and with the positive \(S = 2n_{\mathrm{x}} n_{\mathrm{y}} = 0{,}8\) the normal is \((2, 1, 0)/\sqrt5\), the same as above. The largest shear stress among the faces perpendicular to the plate is the radius, 50 MPa, on the faces with \(\sigma_{\mathrm{n}} = 60\) MPa. These are the faces with the normals \((\vek e_1 + \vek e_2)/\sqrt2 = (1, 3, 0)/\sqrt{10}\) and \((\vek e_1 - \vek e_2)/\sqrt2 = (3, -1, 0)/\sqrt{10}\), halfway between the principal directions \(\vek e_1\) and \(\vek e_2\). We check the first: \(\vek t = \ten\sigma\,\vek n = (210, 130, 0)/\sqrt{10}\), \(\sigma_{\mathrm{n}} = (210 + 390)/10 = 60\) MPa, \(|\vek t|^2 = (44\,100 + 16\,900)/10 = 6100\) MPa², and \(\tau^2 = 6100 - 60^2 = 2500\) MPa², so \(\tau = 50\) MPa.

But theorem 2.70 gave 55 MPa, not 50 MPa. There is no contradiction. The circle in figure 2.81 covers only the faces that contain the direction of the axis \(z\), and the two faces with the largest shear do not contain it. We may also use lemma 2.71 on Mohr's circle in principal axes, for the faces turning about any principal direction, since there all shear components are zero and the condition of the lemma holds. This gives three circles (figure 2.82). The faces that contain the direction \(\vek e_3 = \vek e_{\mathrm{z}}\) give the circle through \(\sigma_2 = 10\) and \(\sigma_1 = 110\) MPa, which we have already drawn. The faces that contain the direction \(\vek e_2\) give the circle through \(\sigma_3 = 0\) and \(\sigma_1 = 110\) MPa, with radius \(55\) MPa. The faces that contain the direction \(\vek e_1\) give a small circle through \(0\) and \(10\) MPa, with radius \(5\) MPa. The largest radius belongs to the circle between the largest and the smallest principal stress, and this radius is \(\tau_{\max} = (\sigma_1 - \sigma_3)/2\) of the theorem. SADD shows even more: the points of all faces through \(P\), not only of those that contain a principal direction, lie in the region inside the largest circle and outside both smaller ones (SADD (3.4.10), figure 3.7, PDF p. 71). We will prove this below, with the weights of section 2.12.1.

Why exactly this region? Recall how in section 2.12.1 we wrote the stresses on a face with the unit normal \(\vek n\), whose components in the principal axes are \(n_1\), \(n_2\) and \(n_3\). With the weights \(w_{\mathrm{i}} = n_{\mathrm{i}}^2\), which are not negative and have the sum \(1\), the normal stress \(\sigma_{\mathrm{n}} = \sum_{\mathrm{i}} w_{\mathrm{i}}\sigma_{\mathrm{i}}\) is the weighted average of the principal stresses, and the square of the shear stress is \(\tau^2 = \sum_{\mathrm{i}} w_{\mathrm{i}}\sigma_{\mathrm{i}}^2 - \sigma_{\mathrm{n}}^2\) ((2.66)). The point \((\sigma_{\mathrm{n}}, \tau)\) has two coordinates, and the weights are three numbers with the sum \(1\), so two of them are free. We therefore expect the points of all faces not to lie on the circles only, but to fill a region of the plane. Where its boundary is, a single computation tells: the expression \(\tau^2 + (\sigma_{\mathrm{n}} - \sigma_2)(\sigma_{\mathrm{n}} - \sigma_3)\) equals the weight \(w_1\) times a number that depends on the principal stresses only.

Lemma 2.72 Region of Mohr's circles (območje Mohrovih krogov)

Let \(\sigma_1 \ge \sigma_2 \ge \sigma_3\) be the principal stresses at a point \(P\) of a body in equilibrium and \(\vek e_1\), \(\vek e_2\), \(\vek e_3\) mutually perpendicular unit vectors of the corresponding principal directions. Let the unit normal \(\vek n\) of a plane face through \(P\) have the components \(n_1\), \(n_2\) and \(n_3\) in the principal axes, and let \(\sigma_{\mathrm{n}}\) be the normal and \(\tau\) the shear stress on this face. Then:

  1. The equalities and inequalities
    \[\begin{aligned} \tau^2 + (\sigma_{\mathrm{n}} - \sigma_2)(\sigma_{\mathrm{n}} - \sigma_3) &= n_1^2\,(\sigma_1 - \sigma_2)(\sigma_1 - \sigma_3) \ge 0 , \\ \tau^2 + (\sigma_{\mathrm{n}} - \sigma_3)(\sigma_{\mathrm{n}} - \sigma_1) &= n_2^2\,(\sigma_2 - \sigma_3)(\sigma_2 - \sigma_1) \le 0 , \\ \tau^2 + (\sigma_{\mathrm{n}} - \sigma_1)(\sigma_{\mathrm{n}} - \sigma_2) &= n_3^2\,(\sigma_3 - \sigma_1)(\sigma_3 - \sigma_2) \ge 0 \end{aligned} \tag{2.70}\]
    hold.
  2. For numbers \(a\) and \(b\), let the circle through \(a\) and \(b\) be the circle with centre \(\big((a + b)/2,\ 0\big)\) and radius \(|a - b|/2\) in the plane with the normal stress on the horizontal and the shear stress on the vertical axis. The point \((\sigma_{\mathrm{n}}, \tau)\) lies on or inside the circle through \(\sigma_3\) and \(\sigma_1\), and on or outside the circles through \(\sigma_3\) and \(\sigma_2\) and through \(\sigma_2\) and \(\sigma_1\).
Proof

We must show the three equalities, the signs on the right and the meaning of the inequalities. We write the weights as \(w_{\mathrm{i}} = n_{\mathrm{i}}^2\), and the index \(i\) runs over \(1\), \(2\) and \(3\).

1. Equalities and signs.

  1. The weights are not negative, since they are squares, and by step 7 of the proof of corollary 2.63 on stress in principal axes, \(w_1 + w_2 + w_3 = 1\). By (2.66), \(\sigma_{\mathrm{n}} = \sum_{\mathrm{i}} w_{\mathrm{i}}\sigma_{\mathrm{i}}\) and \(\tau^2 = \sum_{\mathrm{i}} w_{\mathrm{i}}\sigma_{\mathrm{i}}^2 - \sigma_{\mathrm{n}}^2\).
  2. We write the product out as a product of brackets: \((\sigma_{\mathrm{n}} - \sigma_2)(\sigma_{\mathrm{n}} - \sigma_3) = \sigma_{\mathrm{n}}^2 - (\sigma_2 + \sigma_3)\,\sigma_{\mathrm{n}} + \sigma_2\sigma_3\). When we add \(\tau^2\) from step 1, the terms \(-\sigma_{\mathrm{n}}^2\) and \(\sigma_{\mathrm{n}}^2\) cancel:
    \[\tau^2 + (\sigma_{\mathrm{n}} - \sigma_2)(\sigma_{\mathrm{n}} - \sigma_3) = \sum_{\mathrm{i}} w_{\mathrm{i}}\sigma_{\mathrm{i}}^2 - (\sigma_2 + \sigma_3)\,\sigma_{\mathrm{n}} + \sigma_2\sigma_3 .\]
  3. We insert \(\sigma_{\mathrm{n}} = \sum_{\mathrm{i}} w_{\mathrm{i}}\sigma_{\mathrm{i}}\) and \(\sigma_2\sigma_3 = \sigma_2\sigma_3\sum_{\mathrm{i}} w_{\mathrm{i}}\), which we may, since the weights have the sum \(1\). We gather all three terms into one sum over \(i\):
    \[\begin{aligned} \tau^2 + (\sigma_{\mathrm{n}} - \sigma_2)(\sigma_{\mathrm{n}} - \sigma_3) &= \sum_{\mathrm{i}} w_{\mathrm{i}}\,\big(\sigma_{\mathrm{i}}^2 - (\sigma_2 + \sigma_3)\,\sigma_{\mathrm{i}} + \sigma_2\sigma_3\big) \\ &= \sum_{\mathrm{i}} w_{\mathrm{i}}\,(\sigma_{\mathrm{i}} - \sigma_2)(\sigma_{\mathrm{i}} - \sigma_3) , \end{aligned}\]
    where the last bracket is the written-out product as in step 2.
  4. For \(i = 2\) the factor \(\sigma_{\mathrm{i}} - \sigma_2\) is zero, for \(i = 3\) the factor \(\sigma_{\mathrm{i}} - \sigma_3\). Only the term with \(i = 1\) remains, \(w_1\,(\sigma_1 - \sigma_2)(\sigma_1 - \sigma_3)\). This is the first equality.
  5. We repeat steps 2 to 4 with the pairs \(\sigma_3\), \(\sigma_1\) and \(\sigma_1\), \(\sigma_2\) instead of \(\sigma_2\), \(\sigma_3\). Only the term with \(i = 2\) or with \(i = 3\) remains in the sum, and we get the second and the third equality.
  6. Signs. The weights are not negative. Since \(\sigma_1 \ge \sigma_2 \ge \sigma_3\), the numbers \(\sigma_1 - \sigma_2\) and \(\sigma_1 - \sigma_3\) are nonnegative, so the right-hand side of the first equality is not negative. The number \(\sigma_2 - \sigma_3\) is not negative and \(\sigma_2 - \sigma_1\) is not positive, so the right-hand side of the second equality is not positive. The numbers \(\sigma_3 - \sigma_1\) and \(\sigma_3 - \sigma_2\) are not positive, and their product is not negative, so the right-hand side of the third equality is not negative.

2. Meaning of the inequalities.

  1. Let \(a\) and \(b\) be numbers, \(c = (a + b)/2\) and \(d = (a - b)/2\). Then \(a = c + d\) and \(b = c - d\), and by the school formula for the product of a sum and a difference,
    \[(\sigma_{\mathrm{n}} - a)(\sigma_{\mathrm{n}} - b) = \big((\sigma_{\mathrm{n}} - c) - d\big)\big((\sigma_{\mathrm{n}} - c) + d\big) = (\sigma_{\mathrm{n}} - c)^2 - d^2 .\]
  2. So \(\tau^2 + (\sigma_{\mathrm{n}} - a)(\sigma_{\mathrm{n}} - b) = (\sigma_{\mathrm{n}} - c)^2 + \tau^2 - d^2\). By (1.10), \((\sigma_{\mathrm{n}} - c)^2 + \tau^2\) is the square of the distance of the point \((\sigma_{\mathrm{n}}, \tau)\) from the centre \((c, 0)\) of the circle through \(a\) and \(b\), and \(d^2\) is the square of its radius \(|d|\).
  3. The expression of step 8 is not negative exactly when the square of the distance is not smaller than the square of the radius. Both numbers are nonnegative, so by lemma 1.28, that a larger nonnegative number has a larger square, this happens exactly when the distance is not smaller than the radius, when the point is on or outside the circle. In the same way the expression is not positive exactly when the point is on or inside the circle.
  4. The first and the third inequality of item 1 therefore say that the point \((\sigma_{\mathrm{n}}, \tau)\) is on or outside the circle through \(\sigma_2\) and \(\sigma_3\) and on or outside the circle through \(\sigma_1\) and \(\sigma_2\), and the second says that it is on or inside the circle through \(\sigma_3\) and \(\sigma_1\).

Source: SADD (3.4.7)-(3.4.10), figure 3.7 (PDF pp. 70-71). SADD solves the three equations for \(n_1^2\), \(n_2^2\) and \(n_3^2\) and assumes distinct principal stresses for this. The proof with the equalities is not from the source.

The proof showed why the lemma holds. Each of the three expressions is the weighted average of the numbers \((\sigma_{\mathrm{i}} - \sigma_{\mathrm{a}})(\sigma_{\mathrm{i}} - \sigma_{\mathrm{b}})\) with the weights \(w_{\mathrm{i}}\), and for two of the three principal stresses this number is zero. A single term remains, whose sign is fixed by the order of the principal stresses alone. We divided by nothing, so the lemma also holds when two principal stresses are equal. Then two circles merge, for instance in the bar pulled by an axial force, with \(\sigma_2 = \sigma_3 = 0\), where the circle through \(\sigma_2\) and \(\sigma_3\) shrinks to a point and the circles through \(\sigma_3\) and \(\sigma_1\) and through \(\sigma_2\) and \(\sigma_1\) are the same circle. The region is then just this circle, the Mohr circle of the bar of figure 2.80. SADD goes another way: when the principal stresses are distinct, it divides the equalities (2.70) by the nonzero numbers on the right and so computes all three weights from the point \((\sigma_{\mathrm{n}}, \tau)\) (SADD (3.4.9), PDF p. 71). Since only \(\tau^2\) appears in the inequalities, they hold in the same way for the point \((\sigma_{\mathrm{n}}, -\tau)\), which is why we drew the region symmetric in figure 2.82.

Let us test the lemma on the thin plate, for which we found \(\sigma_1 = 110\) MPa, \(\sigma_2 = 10\) MPa and \(\sigma_3 = 0\) with the principal directions \(\vek e_1 = (2, 1, 0)/\sqrt5\), \(\vek e_2 = (-1, 2, 0)/\sqrt5\) and \(\vek e_3 = \vek e_{\mathrm{z}}\). Take the face whose normal points in the direction of the fly's flight, \(\vek n = (1, 2, -2)/3\). Its components in the principal axes are the scalar products with the principal directions (lemma 2.38), \(n_1 = 4/(3\sqrt5)\), \(n_2 = 3/(3\sqrt5)\) and \(n_3 = -2/3\), and the weights are \(w_1 = \tfrac{16}{45}\), \(w_2 = \tfrac{9}{45}\) and \(w_3 = \tfrac{20}{45}\), with the sum \(1\). By (2.66), \(\sigma_{\mathrm{n}} = (110 \cdot 16 + 10 \cdot 9)/45 = 41{,}11\) MPa and \(\tau^2 = 2632{,}1\) MPa², so \(\tau = 51{,}30\) MPa. The three expressions of (2.70) are, in MPa²,

\[\begin{aligned} 2632{,}1 + 31{,}11 \cdot 41{,}11 &= 3911{,}1 = \tfrac{16}{45} \cdot 100 \cdot 110 , \\ 2632{,}1 + 41{,}11 \cdot (-68{,}89) &= -200{,}0 = \tfrac{9}{45} \cdot 10 \cdot (-100) , \\ 2632{,}1 + (-68{,}89) \cdot 31{,}11 &= 488{,}9 = \tfrac{20}{45} \cdot (-110) \cdot (-10) , \end{aligned}\]

as the lemma says, with the signs \(+\), \(-\), \(+\). The point \(B\) in figure 2.83 is this face. The same figure shows the face with the normal \(\vek e_{\mathrm{x}}\), which lies on the blue circle, the face with the weights of figure 2.76, the face with the largest shear stress, and 220 randomly chosen faces, whose points we computed with NumPy. No point lies outside the region.

Mohr's circle is a tool for faces that turn about one axis. SADD remarks that it can be used for computations in a plane, while for general computations the rule for turning the axes is used (SADD, PDF p. 72), which we derived in section 2.9. The thin plate shows why a circle in one plane is not enough: the circle of the faces perpendicular to the plate gives 50 MPa, while the largest shear is 55 MPa on faces that cut the plate obliquely through its thickness.

2.12.4 Spherical and deviatoric parts of stress

In a fluid at rest the traction vector on every face is \(-p\,\vek n\), all three principal stresses are \(-p\), and there is no shear stress anywhere. What happens if we add such a stress, equal pressure from all sides, to some other stress, for example the stress in the plate? Then the new stress matrix is \(\ten\sigma - p\,\mat I\), where \(\mat I\) is the identity matrix. By Cauchy's formula in components (2.24) the traction vector on every face changes by \(-p\,\vek n\). The normal stress on every face therefore decreases by \(p\), because \((-p\,\vek n)\cdot\vek n = -p\), while the shear part \(\vek t - \sigma_{\mathrm{n}}\vek n\) stays the same, because \(\vek t\) and \(\sigma_{\mathrm{n}}\vek n\) change by the same vector \(-p\,\vek n\). The shear on any face does not depend on how much equal pressure or equal tension on all faces the stress contains.

We therefore split the stress into two parts: a part that pulls or pushes equally on all faces, and a remainder. How much equal pull should we take away? The natural choice is the average of the three normal stresses on the faces perpendicular to the axes. This number is the same in all rectangular Cartesian coordinate systems, since it is a third of the first invariant \(I_1 = \sigma_{\mathrm{xx}} + \sigma_{\mathrm{yy}} + \sigma_{\mathrm{zz}}\) of definition 2.65, which by lemma 2.66 does not change when the axes turn. In principal axes it is therefore \((\sigma_1 + \sigma_2 + \sigma_3)/3\).

Definition 2.73 Spherical and deviatoric parts of stress (sferični in deviatorni del napetosti)

Let \(\ten\sigma\) be the symmetric matrix of the stress components at a point \(P\) in a chosen rectangular Cartesian coordinate system. The mean stress (srednja napetost) at \(P\) is the number

\[\sigma_{\mathrm{m}} = \frac{\sigma_{\mathrm{xx}} + \sigma_{\mathrm{yy}} + \sigma_{\mathrm{zz}}}{3} = \frac{I_1}{3} . \tag{2.71}\]

The spherical part (sferični del) of the stress is the matrix \(\sigma_{\mathrm{m}}\,\mat I\). The deviatoric part or deviator (deviatorni del, deviator) of the stress is the matrix

\[\ten s = \ten\sigma - \sigma_{\mathrm{m}}\,\mat I , \tag{2.72}\]

with the components \(s_{\mathrm{xx}} = \sigma_{\mathrm{xx}} - \sigma_{\mathrm{m}}\), \(s_{\mathrm{yy}} = \sigma_{\mathrm{yy}} - \sigma_{\mathrm{m}}\), \(s_{\mathrm{zz}} = \sigma_{\mathrm{zz}} - \sigma_{\mathrm{m}}\) and \(s_{\mathrm{ij}} = \sigma_{\mathrm{ij}}\) when the indices \(i\) and \(j\) are different. Here the indices \(i\) and \(j\) run over \(x\), \(y\), \(z\). The second deviatoric invariant (druga invarianta deviatorja) is the number

\[J_2 = \frac12\sum_{\mathrm{i}}\sum_{\mathrm{j}} s_{\mathrm{ij}}^2 . \tag{2.73}\]

Source: CM (4.3.14)-(4.3.17) (PDF p. 189), SADD (3.5.1)-(3.5.3) (PDF pp. 72-73), BOWER §2.2.7 (PDF p. 75). CM writes the number \(J_2\) as \(I'_2\), BOWER as \(J_2\) (PDF p. 117).

The matrix \(\ten\sigma - \sigma_{\mathrm{m}}\mat I\) is computed entry by entry, like the sum of matrices in section 1.16: we subtract \(\sigma_{\mathrm{m}}\) from each diagonal entry, and the others stay. The name spherical part says that this part acts equally on all faces, in all directions, like the pressure in a fluid with \(p = -\sigma_{\mathrm{m}}\). CM also calls it the hydrostatic part (hidrostatični del) (CM, PDF p. 189). The name deviator says that this part measures how much the stress deviates from an equal pull in all directions. The books write the deviator differently: CM \(\ten\sigma'\), SADD \(\hat\sigma_{\mathrm{ij}}\), BOWER \(\sigma'_{\mathrm{ij}}\) (CM (4.3.16), SADD (3.5.2), BOWER, PDF p. 75). We write \(\ten s\), because we keep the prime for derivatives.

Lemma 2.74 Properties of the deviator (lastnosti deviatorja)

Let \(\ten s\) be the deviator of the symmetric stress matrix \(\ten\sigma\) at a point \(P\) and \(\sigma_{\mathrm{m}}\) the mean stress. Then:

  1. \(s_{\mathrm{xx}} + s_{\mathrm{yy}} + s_{\mathrm{zz}} = 0\).
  2. For every unit normal \(\vek n\), \(\vek t(\vek n) = \ten s\,\vek n + \sigma_{\mathrm{m}}\,\vek n\). The normal stress on the face is larger by \(\sigma_{\mathrm{m}}\) than the number \((\ten s\,\vek n)\cdot\vek n\), while the shear part of the traction vector equals \(\ten s\,\vek n - \big((\ten s\,\vek n)\cdot\vek n\big)\,\vek n\) and does not depend on \(\sigma_{\mathrm{m}}\).
  3. If \(\vek e\) is a principal direction of the stress with principal stress \(\sigma_{\mathrm{i}}\), then \(\ten s\,\vek e = (\sigma_{\mathrm{i}} - \sigma_{\mathrm{m}})\,\vek e\). The deviator has the same principal directions as the stress, and its eigenvalues are \(s_{\mathrm{i}} = \sigma_{\mathrm{i}} - \sigma_{\mathrm{m}}\).
Proof

All three items follow from the fact that the deviator differs from the stress only on the diagonal, by \(\sigma_{\mathrm{m}}\).

1. Sum of the diagonal entries.

  1. By definition \(s_{\mathrm{xx}} + s_{\mathrm{yy}} + s_{\mathrm{zz}} = \sigma_{\mathrm{xx}} + \sigma_{\mathrm{yy}} + \sigma_{\mathrm{zz}} - 3\sigma_{\mathrm{m}}\).
  2. By (2.71) \(3\sigma_{\mathrm{m}} = \sigma_{\mathrm{xx}} + \sigma_{\mathrm{yy}} + \sigma_{\mathrm{zz}}\), so the sum is zero.

2. The traction vector.

  1. The stress is symmetric (theorem 2.36), so by (2.42) \(\vek t(\vek n) = \ten\sigma\,\vek n\). The \(x\) component is \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xx}} n_{\mathrm{x}} + \sigma_{\mathrm{xy}} n_{\mathrm{y}} + \sigma_{\mathrm{xz}} n_{\mathrm{z}}\).
  2. We insert \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xx}} = s_{\mathrm{xx}} + \sigma_{\mathrm{m}}\), \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xy}} = s_{\mathrm{xy}}\) and \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xz}} = s_{\mathrm{xz}}\). The \(x\) component is \(s_{\mathrm{xx}} n_{\mathrm{x}} + s_{\mathrm{xy}} n_{\mathrm{y}} + s_{\mathrm{xz}} n_{\mathrm{z}} + \sigma_{\mathrm{m}} n_{\mathrm{x}}\), which is the \(x\) component of the vector \(\ten s\,\vek n\) increased by \(\sigma_{\mathrm{m}} n_{\mathrm{x}}\). Likewise for the \(y\) and \(z\) components. Hence \(\vek t(\vek n) = \ten s\,\vek n + \sigma_{\mathrm{m}}\,\vek n\).
  3. By the rules of the scalar product the normal stress is \(\sigma_{\mathrm{n}} = (\ten s\,\vek n)\cdot\vek n + \sigma_{\mathrm{m}}\,(\vek n\cdot\vek n) = (\ten s\,\vek n)\cdot\vek n + \sigma_{\mathrm{m}}\), because \(\vek n\) is a unit vector.
  4. The shear part is \(\vek t(\vek n) - \sigma_{\mathrm{n}}\vek n = \ten s\,\vek n + \sigma_{\mathrm{m}}\vek n - \big((\ten s\,\vek n)\cdot\vek n\big)\,\vek n - \sigma_{\mathrm{m}}\vek n\). The terms with \(\sigma_{\mathrm{m}}\) cancel.

3. Principal directions.

  1. By definition 2.60 \(\ten\sigma\,\vek e = \sigma_{\mathrm{i}}\,\vek e\).
  2. By step 2 of item 2, applied to the normal \(\vek e\), \(\ten s\,\vek e = \ten\sigma\,\vek e - \sigma_{\mathrm{m}}\vek e = (\sigma_{\mathrm{i}} - \sigma_{\mathrm{m}})\,\vek e\).
  3. Conversely, let \(\ten s\,\vek v = \mu\,\vek v\) for some nonzero vector \(\vek v\). We compute the components of \(\ten\sigma\,\vek v\) as in step 2 of item 2, only with \(\vek v\) in place of \(\vek n\), so \(\ten\sigma\,\vek v = \ten s\,\vek v + \sigma_{\mathrm{m}}\vek v = (\mu + \sigma_{\mathrm{m}})\,\vek v\).
  4. By lemma 1.97 on the linearity of the product with a matrix also \(\ten\sigma\,(\vek v/|\vek v|) = (\mu + \sigma_{\mathrm{m}})\,\vek v/|\vek v|\), so the unit vector \(\vek v/|\vek v|\) is a principal direction of the stress with the principal stress \(\mu + \sigma_{\mathrm{m}}\). By corollary 2.67 on the principal stresses as the roots of the characteristic equation this is one of the numbers \(\sigma_{\mathrm{i}}\), so \(\mu = \sigma_{\mathrm{i}} - \sigma_{\mathrm{m}}\) for some \(i\).

Source: CM (4.3.15), (4.3.16) (PDF p. 189). SADD states that the deviator and the stress have the same principal directions and leaves the proof to exercise 3.15 (SADD, PDF p. 73). The proof is not from the sources.

The lemma says what the two parts mean. The spherical part pulls or pushes equally on every face, by \(\sigma_{\mathrm{m}}\), and has no shear. The deviator carries all the shear, since the shear part on every face depends only on it. Its diagonal entries add up to zero, so on average it neither pulls nor pushes. BOWER puts it in words: the mean stress is a measure of the pressure exerted by the stress, and pressure tends to change the volume of a piece of material, while the deviator is a measure of the shearing, which tends to change the shape of the piece without changing its volume (BOWER §2.2.7, PDF p. 75). How exactly this happens depends on the material, and for a material that behaves the same in all directions we will see it in chapter 3. Why the split matters is shown by experiment: equal pressure from all sides, however large, does not make a metal yield (BOWER §3.7.3, PDF p. 146). What decides yielding is the deviator.

Let us split the stress in the thin plate. The mean stress is \(\sigma_{\mathrm{m}} = (90 + 30 + 0)/3 = 40\) MPa, and the deviator is

\[\ten s = \begin{pmatrix} 90 - 40 & 40 & 0 \\ 40 & 30 - 40 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 - 40 \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} 50 & 40 & 0 \\ 40 & -10 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & -40 \end{pmatrix}\ \text{MPa} .\]

The diagonal adds up to \(50 - 10 - 40 = 0\), as item 1 of the lemma says. By item 3 the principal values of the deviator are \(110 - 40 = 70\) MPa, \(10 - 40 = -30\) MPa and \(0 - 40 = -40\) MPa, along the same directions as the principal stresses. Figure 2.84 shows the split on a small cube with faces perpendicular to the principal directions. A cube pulled by \(110\) MPa in one direction and \(10\) MPa in another equals a cube pulled equally by \(40\) MPa from all sides plus a cube pulled by \(70\) MPa along \(\vek e_1\) and compressed by \(30\) MPa and \(40\) MPa in the other two directions.

For the bar with the stress \(\sigma\), \(\sigma_{\mathrm{m}} = \sigma/3\), and the principal values of the deviator are \(2\sigma/3\), \(-\sigma/3\) and \(-\sigma/3\). So even simple tension has a spherical part, a third of the stress. In pure shear \(\sigma_{\mathrm{m}} = (0 + 0 + 0)/3 = 0\), and the deviator is the whole stress. In a fluid at rest \(\sigma_{\mathrm{m}} = -p\) and the deviator is the zero matrix: the stress is its spherical part alone.

The question remains how to say with one number how much shear the deviator carries. This is what the second deviatoric invariant \(J_2\) of the definition is for. It is half the sum of the squares of all nine components of the deviator, so it is never negative, and it is zero only when the deviator is the zero matrix. The next lemma says that it does not depend on the choice of axes and expresses it by the principal stresses.

Lemma 2.75 Expressions for the second deviatoric invariant (izrazi za drugo invarianto deviatorja)

Let \(\ten s\) be the deviator of the symmetric stress matrix \(\ten\sigma\) with the principal stresses \(\sigma_1\), \(\sigma_2\) and \(\sigma_3\), and \(I_1\) and \(I_2\) the invariants of the matrix \(\ten\sigma\) of definition 2.65. Then

\[\begin{aligned} J_2 &= \frac12\,(s_{\mathrm{xx}}^2 + s_{\mathrm{yy}}^2 + s_{\mathrm{zz}}^2) + s_{\mathrm{xy}}^2 + s_{\mathrm{yz}}^2 + s_{\mathrm{zx}}^2 \\ &= \frac{I_1^2}{3} - I_2 = \frac16\Big((\sigma_1 - \sigma_2)^2 + (\sigma_2 - \sigma_3)^2 + (\sigma_3 - \sigma_1)^2\Big) , \end{aligned} \tag{2.74}\]

and \(J_2\) has the same value in all rectangular Cartesian coordinate systems.

Proof

We get the first expression by writing out the sum, the second with the invariants \(I_1\) and \(I_2\), the third in principal axes.

  1. The double sum in (2.73) has nine terms. Three are diagonal, \(s_{\mathrm{xx}}^2\), \(s_{\mathrm{yy}}^2\) and \(s_{\mathrm{zz}}^2\). The remaining six are equal in pairs, since \(s_{\mathrm{xy}} = \sigma_{\mathrm{xy}} = \sigma_{\mathrm{yx}} = s_{\mathrm{yx}}\) by the symmetry of stress, and likewise for the other two pairs. Half the sum is therefore the first expression in (2.74).
  2. We express the diagonal terms by the stress. We write out \((\sigma_{\mathrm{xx}} - \sigma_{\mathrm{m}})^2 = \sigma_{\mathrm{xx}}^2 - 2\sigma_{\mathrm{m}}\sigma_{\mathrm{xx}} + \sigma_{\mathrm{m}}^2\), likewise for \(y\) and \(z\), and add. Since \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xx}} + \sigma_{\mathrm{yy}} + \sigma_{\mathrm{zz}} = 3\sigma_{\mathrm{m}}\), the sum is \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xx}}^2 + \sigma_{\mathrm{yy}}^2 + \sigma_{\mathrm{zz}}^2 - 6\sigma_{\mathrm{m}}^2 + 3\sigma_{\mathrm{m}}^2 = \sigma_{\mathrm{xx}}^2 + \sigma_{\mathrm{yy}}^2 + \sigma_{\mathrm{zz}}^2 - 3\sigma_{\mathrm{m}}^2\).
  3. With \(\sigma_{\mathrm{m}} = I_1/3\), \(3\sigma_{\mathrm{m}}^2 = I_1^2/3\). The off-diagonal entries of \(\ten s\) and \(\ten\sigma\) are equal, so \(\sum_{\mathrm{i}}\sum_{\mathrm{j}} s_{\mathrm{ij}}^2 = \sum_{\mathrm{i}}\sum_{\mathrm{j}} \sigma_{\mathrm{ij}}^2 - I_1^2/3\).
  4. The sum of the squares of all nine stress components is the trace (the sum of the diagonal entries) of the matrix \(\ten\sigma\ten\sigma\). By the rule for the matrix product, the diagonal entry is \((\ten\sigma\ten\sigma)_{\mathrm{xx}} = \sigma_{\mathrm{xx}}\sigma_{\mathrm{xx}} + \sigma_{\mathrm{xy}}\sigma_{\mathrm{yx}} + \sigma_{\mathrm{xz}}\sigma_{\mathrm{zx}} = \sigma_{\mathrm{xx}}^2 + \sigma_{\mathrm{xy}}^2 + \sigma_{\mathrm{xz}}^2\), because \(\ten\sigma\) is symmetric. Likewise \((\ten\sigma\ten\sigma)_{\mathrm{yy}}\) and \((\ten\sigma\ten\sigma)_{\mathrm{zz}}\) are the sums of the squares of the second and the third row, and the sum of all three is \(\sum_{\mathrm{i}}\sum_{\mathrm{j}}\sigma_{\mathrm{ij}}^2\).
  5. As we showed for definition 2.65, \(I_2 = \tfrac12\big(I_1^2 - \tr(\ten\sigma\ten\sigma)\big)\), so \(\tr(\ten\sigma\ten\sigma) = I_1^2 - 2I_2\).
  6. From steps 3 to 5, \(J_2 = \tfrac12\big(I_1^2 - 2I_2 - I_1^2/3\big) = I_1^2/3 - I_2\).
  7. By lemma 2.66, \(I_1\) and \(I_2\) do not change when the axes turn, so neither does \(J_2\).
  8. In principal axes the stress matrix is diagonal, with \(\sigma_1\), \(\sigma_2\) and \(\sigma_3\) on the diagonal. There \(I_1 = \sigma_1 + \sigma_2 + \sigma_3\) and \(\tr(\ten\sigma\ten\sigma) = \sigma_1^2 + \sigma_2^2 + \sigma_3^2\), so by step 5 \(I_2 = \tfrac12\big((\sigma_1 + \sigma_2 + \sigma_3)^2 - \sigma_1^2 - \sigma_2^2 - \sigma_3^2\big) = \sigma_1\sigma_2 + \sigma_2\sigma_3 + \sigma_3\sigma_1\).
  9. By step 6, therefore,
    \[J_2 = \frac{\sigma_1^2 + \sigma_2^2 + \sigma_3^2 + 2(\sigma_1\sigma_2 + \sigma_2\sigma_3 + \sigma_3\sigma_1)}{3} - (\sigma_1\sigma_2 + \sigma_2\sigma_3 + \sigma_3\sigma_1) = \frac{\sigma_1^2 + \sigma_2^2 + \sigma_3^2 - \sigma_1\sigma_2 - \sigma_2\sigma_3 - \sigma_3\sigma_1}{3} .\]
  10. Writing out the squares gives \((\sigma_1 - \sigma_2)^2 + (\sigma_2 - \sigma_3)^2 + (\sigma_3 - \sigma_1)^2 = 2(\sigma_1^2 + \sigma_2^2 + \sigma_3^2) - 2(\sigma_1\sigma_2 + \sigma_2\sigma_3 + \sigma_3\sigma_1)\), which is twice the numerator of step 9. So \(J_2\) is a sixth of this sum.

Source: The first expression: BOWER (PDF p. 117), where \(J_2 = (\sigma_{\mathrm{ij}}\sigma_{\mathrm{ij}} - \sigma_{\mathrm{kk}}\sigma_{\mathrm{pp}}/3)/2\). The expression with the principal stresses follows from SADD (3.5.4) and (3.5.5) (PDF p. 73). The proof is not from the sources.

The third expression in (2.74) contains only differences of the principal stresses. If we add the same number to all three, \(J_2\) does not change, which is another way of saying that the spherical part carries no shear. For the plate the principal stresses are \(110\), \(10\) and \(0\) MPa, and the third expression gives \(J_2 = (100^2 + 10^2 + 110^2)/6 = 22\,200/6 = 3700\) MPa². The first expression with the components of the deviator gives the same, \(\tfrac12\,(50^2 + 10^2 + 40^2) + 40^2 = 2100 + 1600 = 3700\) MPa². So does the second: \(I_1 = 120\) MPa, \(I_2 = 90 \cdot 30 - 40^2 = 1100\) MPa², and \(120^2/3 - 1100 = 3700\) MPa².

The third deviatoric invariant (tretja invarianta deviatorja) is \(J_3 = \det\ten s\). It does not change when the axes turn, for the same reason as \(I_3 = \det\ten\sigma\) in lemma 2.66, since the deviator changes by the same rule as the stress when the axes turn. By the definition, the deviator in the turned axes is \(\bar{\ten s} = \bar{\ten\sigma} - \bar\sigma_{\mathrm{m}}\mat I\), where \(\bar\sigma_{\mathrm{m}} = \bar I_1/3\). By lemma 2.66 \(\bar I_1 = I_1\), so \(\bar\sigma_{\mathrm{m}} = \sigma_{\mathrm{m}}\). By (2.44) \(\bar{\ten\sigma} = \mat Q\ten\sigma\mat Q^\T\), and by lemma 2.40 on the orthogonality of the rotation matrix \(\mat I = \mat Q\mat Q^\T\). Therefore \(\bar{\ten s} = \mat Q\ten\sigma\mat Q^\T - \sigma_{\mathrm{m}}\,\mat Q\mat Q^\T = \mat Q\,(\ten\sigma - \sigma_{\mathrm{m}}\mat I)\,\mat Q^\T = \mat Q\,\ten s\,\mat Q^\T\), where we wrote \(\sigma_{\mathrm{m}}\,\mat Q\mat Q^\T\) as \(\mat Q\,(\sigma_{\mathrm{m}}\mat I)\,\mat Q^\T\), as in step 2 of the proof of lemma 2.66. In principal axes \(J_3 = s_1 s_2 s_3\), for the plate \(70 \cdot (-30) \cdot (-40) = 84\,000\) MPa³. We will not need it in the rest of the chapter.

2.12.5 The von Mises equivalent stress

In section 2.2 we defined the yield stress \(\sigma_{\mathrm{Y}}\) with a bar in tension and said that we would treat yielding under loading in several directions later. Now we have the tools at least for the question how to compare the stress at a point with the number \(\sigma_{\mathrm{Y}}\). We are looking for one number, computed from the stress at the point, that for a bar in tension equals the stress \(\sigma\) in the cross section. Experiments with metals tell two things (BOWER §3.7.3, PDF p. 146). First, equal pressure from all sides does not cause yielding, so the number should depend only on the deviator. Second, most metals behave the same in all directions, so the number should depend only on the sizes of the principal stresses, not on their directions, that is, it should be the same in all coordinate systems. Both requirements are met by \(J_2\), which depends only on the deviator and by lemma 2.75 is the same in all rectangular Cartesian coordinate systems. But they are also met by the largest shear stress \((\sigma_1 - \sigma_3)/2\) of theorem 2.70. It depends only on the principal stresses, and it does not change when we add the same number to all three. So the requirements do not determine the number, and two yield criteria rest on them, which we write down below (BOWER, PDF p. 146).

The largest shear stress as a measure is older. Coulomb already thought that failure is triggered by shear (section 1.1, TIMO, PDF p. 226). Henri Tresca studied by experiment how metals flow under great pressure. This was then an entirely new field (TIMO, PDF p. 205 and 206). The experiments encouraged Saint-Venant to be the first to write the fundamental equations of plasticity, that is of permanent change of shape, and to apply them in several practical problems (TIMO, PDF p. 205 and 206). From Tresca's experiments he deduced that the difference between the largest and the smallest principal stress is constant (TP2B, PDF p. 320). By theorem 2.70 this difference is twice the largest shear stress, so this means that the largest shear stress at yielding is everywhere the same. LOVE describes this view as a measure of the tendency to rupture (LOVE, PDF p. 140).

The condition with \(J_2\) was proposed in 1904 by Maksymilian Tytus Huber and independently of him in 1913 by R. von Mises (TIMO, PDF p. 308). Why precisely \(J_2\), is shown by the work that the material stores when it changes shape (section 3.6.5).

The condition named after von Mises uses \(J_2\). For a bar in tension the principal stresses are \(\sigma\), \(0\) and \(0\), and by (2.74) \(J_2 = (\sigma^2 + 0 + \sigma^2)/6 = \sigma^2/3\). To get \(\sigma\) we must multiply \(J_2\) by \(3\) and take the square root: \(\sqrt{3 \cdot \sigma^2/3} = |\sigma|\), which in tension, where \(\sigma > 0\), equals \(\sigma\).

Definition 2.76 Von Mises equivalent stress (von Misesova primerjalna napetost)

The von Mises equivalent stress (von Misesova primerjalna napetost) at a point \(P\) is the number

\[\sigma_{\mathrm{vM}} = \sqrt{3 J_2} , \tag{2.75}\]

where \(J_2\) is the second invariant of the deviator of the stress at \(P\).

Source: SADD (3.5.5) (PDF p. 73), BOWER §2.2.7 (PDF p. 75), where \(\sigma_{\mathrm{e}} = \sqrt{\tfrac32\sigma'_{\mathrm{ij}}\sigma'_{\mathrm{ij}}}\).

By lemma 2.75

\[\sigma_{\mathrm{vM}} = \sqrt{\tfrac12\Big((\sigma_1 - \sigma_2)^2 + (\sigma_2 - \sigma_3)^2 + (\sigma_3 - \sigma_1)^2\Big)} ,\]

and in this form SADD and BOWER write it (SADD, PDF p. 73, BOWER, PDF p. 75). The name equivalent stress says what it is for. BOWER describes it as a uniaxial equivalent of a stress in several directions: if a material fails in a tension test at the stress \(\sigma_{\text{crit}}\), it also fails under loading in several directions when \(\sigma_{\mathrm{vM}} = \sigma_{\text{crit}}\) (BOWER, PDF p. 75). The von Mises yield criterion (von Misesov pogoj tečenja) says that the material starts to yield when \(\sigma_{\mathrm{vM}} = \sigma_{\mathrm{Y}}\) (BOWER §3.7.3, PDF p. 145). The Tresca criterion of section 2.4, in turn, compares the largest shear stress with the largest shear stress in a bar in tension at the yield stress, which by theorem 2.70 is \(\sigma_{\mathrm{Y}}/2\). By this criterion the material starts to yield when \(\sigma_1 - \sigma_3 = \sigma_{\mathrm{Y}}\) (BOWER, PDF p. 146). Here we only state the two criteria. What happens to the material once it yields is described by the theory of plasticity (BOWER §3.7, PDF pp. 140-161), which this book does not develop. BOWER says that tests agree somewhat better with the von Mises criterion than with Tresca's, but that the difference between them is very small (BOWER, PDF p. 146).

Let us compute the von Mises stress for our examples, for steel with the yield stress \(\sigma_{\mathrm{Y}} = 220\) MPa.

  1. The bar with diameter 10 mm under the force 10 kN: the principal stresses are \(127{,}3\) MPa, \(0\) and \(0\), and \(\sigma_{\mathrm{vM}} = \sqrt{\tfrac12\,(127{,}3^2 + 0 + 127{,}3^2)} = 127{,}3\) MPa. This is how it must be, since we calibrated the number that way. Also \(\sigma_1 - \sigma_3 = 127{,}3\) MPa. Both criteria say that the bar does not yield, since \(127{,}3 < 220\).
  2. Pure shear with \(\tau_0 = 50\) MPa: the principal stresses are \(50\), \(0\) and \(-50\) MPa, and \(\sigma_{\mathrm{vM}} = \sqrt{\tfrac12\,(50^2 + 50^2 + 100^2)} = \sqrt{3}\cdot 50 = 86{,}6\) MPa, while \(\sigma_1 - \sigma_3 = 100\) MPa. In pure shear, steel would start to yield at \(\tau_0 = 220/\sqrt3 = 127{,}0\) MPa by von Mises and at \(\tau_0 = 220/2 = 110\) MPa by Tresca. Here the two criteria differ by about 15 %.
  3. The thin plate: \(\sigma_{\mathrm{vM}} = \sqrt{3 \cdot 3700} = \sqrt{11\,100} = 105{,}4\) MPa, \(\sigma_1 - \sigma_3 = 110\) MPa. The criteria differ by about 4 %, and by both the plate does not yield.
  4. The fluid at rest: the deviator is the zero matrix, so \(\sigma_{\mathrm{vM}} = 0\) for every pressure \(p\).

The von Mises stress also has a geometric meaning, which SADD gives (SADD, PDF p. 73). In principal axes take the faces whose normals have all three components equal in absolute value.

Definition 2.77 Octahedral plane (oktaedrska ploskev)

Let \(\vek e_1\), \(\vek e_2\) and \(\vek e_3\) be the unit vectors of the principal directions of the stress at a point \(P\). An octahedral plane (oktaedrska ploskev) through \(P\) is a flat face with unit normal

\[\vek n = \frac{\pm\vek e_1 \pm \vek e_2 \pm \vek e_3}{\sqrt3} ,\]

for any choice of signs. The normal and the shear stress on it are called the octahedral normal stress \(\sigma_{\mathrm{oct}}\) and the octahedral shear stress \(\tau_{\mathrm{oct}}\) (oktaedrska normalna in strižna napetost).

Source: SADD §3.5 (PDF p. 73).

The normal is a unit vector, since the sum of the squares of its components is \(\tfrac13 + \tfrac13 + \tfrac13 = 1\). The eight choices of signs give eight normals. If we measure equal distances from \(P\) along the principal axes to both sides and join the six points obtained, we get a solid with eight triangular faces, an octahedron (oktaeder), and its faces have exactly these eight normals (figure 2.85). Hence the name.

Lemma 2.78 Stresses on the octahedral plane (napetosti na oktaedrski ploskvi)

On every octahedral plane through the point \(P\)

\[\sigma_{\mathrm{oct}} = \sigma_{\mathrm{m}} , \qquad \tau_{\mathrm{oct}} = \sqrt{\tfrac23\,J_2} = \frac{\sqrt2}{3}\,\sigma_{\mathrm{vM}} . \tag{2.76}\]
Proof

We use the expressions with weights of section 2.12.1.

  1. All three components of the normal are \(\pm 1/\sqrt3\), so all the weights are \(w_{\mathrm{i}} = n_{\mathrm{i}}^2 = \tfrac13\).
  2. By (2.66) \(\sigma_{\mathrm{oct}} = \tfrac13\,(\sigma_1 + \sigma_2 + \sigma_3)\). By (2.65) the sum of the principal stresses is \(I_1\), so \(\sigma_{\mathrm{oct}} = I_1/3 = \sigma_{\mathrm{m}}\).
  3. By (2.67) \(\tau_{\mathrm{oct}}^2 = \tfrac13\big((\sigma_1 - \sigma_{\mathrm{m}})^2 + (\sigma_2 - \sigma_{\mathrm{m}})^2 + (\sigma_3 - \sigma_{\mathrm{m}})^2\big)\).
  4. By item 3 of lemma 2.74 the differences \(\sigma_{\mathrm{i}} - \sigma_{\mathrm{m}}\) are the principal values \(s_{\mathrm{i}}\) of the deviator. In principal axes the deviator is diagonal, with \(s_1\), \(s_2\) and \(s_3\) on the diagonal, so by (2.73) \(J_2 = \tfrac12\,(s_1^2 + s_2^2 + s_3^2)\), and by lemma 2.75 the value of \(J_2\) in principal axes is the same as in all others.
  5. From steps 3 and 4, \(\tau_{\mathrm{oct}}^2 = \tfrac13 \cdot 2J_2 = \tfrac23\,J_2\).
  6. By (2.75) \(J_2 = \sigma_{\mathrm{vM}}^2/3\), so \(\tau_{\mathrm{oct}} = \sqrt{\tfrac29\,\sigma_{\mathrm{vM}}^2} = \tfrac{\sqrt2}{3}\,\sigma_{\mathrm{vM}}\).

Source: SADD (3.5.4) (PDF p. 73), where \(\sigma_{\mathrm{vM}} = \tfrac{3}{\sqrt2}\,\tau_{\mathrm{oct}}\) is also written. The proof is not from the sources.

On the octahedral planes the normal stress is the mean stress, and the shear stress is proportional to the von Mises stress. The von Mises stress is therefore, up to the factor \(3/\sqrt2 = 2{,}121\), the shear stress on the faces that are equally inclined to all three principal directions. For the thin plate the octahedral normal is \((\vek e_1 + \vek e_2 + \vek e_3)/\sqrt3 = (0{,}2582,\ 0{,}7746,\ 0{,}5774)\) in the axes \(x\), \(y\), \(z\), and the lemma gives \(\sigma_{\mathrm{oct}} = 40\) MPa and \(\tau_{\mathrm{oct}} = \sqrt{\tfrac23 \cdot 3700} = 49{,}67\) MPa. We got the same two numbers with NumPy directly from Cauchy's formula for this normal.

2.12.6 Spherical and deviatoric parts of strain

The strain at a point is described by the small strain tensor \(\ten\varepsilon\), a symmetric matrix with the components \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}}\), \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xy}}\) and so on (section 1.17). It too can be split into a part that is the same in all directions and a remainder. The meaning of the two parts is even more vivid here than for stress, since strain describes the shape of a piece of material.

Definition 2.79 Volumetric, spherical and deviatoric strain (prostorninska, sferična in deviatorna deformacija)

Let \(\ten\varepsilon\) be the small strain tensor at a point \(P\), written with components in a chosen rectangular Cartesian coordinate system. The volumetric strain (prostorninska deformacija) at \(P\) is the number

\[\varepsilon_{\mathrm{v}} = \varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}} + \varepsilon_{\mathrm{yy}} + \varepsilon_{\mathrm{zz}} .\]

The spherical strain (sferični del deformacije) is the matrix \(\tfrac13\,\varepsilon_{\mathrm{v}}\,\mat I\), and the deviatoric part of the strain or deviatoric strain (deviatorna deformacija) is the matrix

\[\ten e = \ten\varepsilon - \tfrac13\,\varepsilon_{\mathrm{v}}\,\mat I , \tag{2.77}\]

with the components \(e_{\mathrm{xx}} = \varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}} - \varepsilon_{\mathrm{v}}/3\), \(e_{\mathrm{yy}} = \varepsilon_{\mathrm{yy}} - \varepsilon_{\mathrm{v}}/3\), \(e_{\mathrm{zz}} = \varepsilon_{\mathrm{zz}} - \varepsilon_{\mathrm{v}}/3\) and \(e_{\mathrm{ij}} = \varepsilon_{\mathrm{ij}}\) for different indices.

Source: SADD (2.5.1)-(2.5.3) (PDF p. 49), BOWER §2.1.9 (PDF p. 51).

The components \(e_{\mathrm{xx}}\), \(e_{\mathrm{xy}}\) and the like have two indices and are not bold, so we do not confuse them with the unit vectors of the axes \(\vek e_{\mathrm{x}}\), \(\vek e_{\mathrm{y}}\) and \(\vek e_{\mathrm{z}}\). SADD calls the volumetric strain the cubical dilatation and writes it \(\vartheta\), and the deviatoric strain \(\hat e_{\mathrm{ij}}\) (SADD, PDF p. 49). The next lemma says what the two parts mean.

Lemma 2.80 Meaning of the spherical and deviatoric strain (pomen sferičnega in deviatornega dela deformacije)

Let the small deformation assumption hold at the point \(P\) (section 1.17.3): all partial derivatives of the displacements are small in absolute value compared with \(1\). Then:

  1. If the strain at \(P\) equals its spherical part, every short fibre through \(P\), whatever its direction, has the strain \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{v}}/3\), and the right angle between two short fibres in perpendicular directions stays right.
  2. The deviatoric strain has zero volumetric strain: \(e_{\mathrm{xx}} + e_{\mathrm{yy}} + e_{\mathrm{zz}} = 0\).
  3. The relative change of volume of a small piece around \(P\) is approximately \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{v}}\).
Proof

We use the strain of a fibre (1.53) and the change of volume of lemma 2.55.

1. The spherical part.

  1. The matrix \(\tfrac13\,\varepsilon_{\mathrm{v}}\,\mat I\) has \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{v}}/3\) on the diagonal and zeros elsewhere.
  2. By (1.53) a fibre in the direction of the unit vector \(\vek n\) has the strain \(\tfrac13\,\varepsilon_{\mathrm{v}}\,(n_{\mathrm{x}}^2 + n_{\mathrm{y}}^2 + n_{\mathrm{z}}^2) = \varepsilon_{\mathrm{v}}/3\), because the terms with two different indices are zero and the sum of the squares of the components of a unit vector is \(1\).
  3. By section 2.9.5 the cosine of the angle between two short fibres in perpendicular directions \(\vek m\) and \(\vek n\) after loading is, to first order, \(2\,\vek m^\T\ten\varepsilon\,\vek n\), and the angle stays right when this number is zero. For \(\ten\varepsilon = \tfrac13\,\varepsilon_{\mathrm{v}}\,\mat I\) we have \(\vek m^\T\ten\varepsilon\,\vek n = \tfrac13\,\varepsilon_{\mathrm{v}}\,(\vek m\cdot\vek n) = 0\), because \(\vek m\) and \(\vek n\) are perpendicular.

2. The deviatoric strain.

  1. By definition \(e_{\mathrm{xx}} + e_{\mathrm{yy}} + e_{\mathrm{zz}} = \varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}} + \varepsilon_{\mathrm{yy}} + \varepsilon_{\mathrm{zz}} - 3 \cdot \varepsilon_{\mathrm{v}}/3 = \varepsilon_{\mathrm{v}} - \varepsilon_{\mathrm{v}} = 0\).

3. The change of volume.

  1. By section 2.10.5 the loading maps a small piece at \(P\) approximately onto the parallelepiped spanned by the vectors of its edges multiplied by the deformation gradient \(\mat F\). By item 1 of lemma 2.55 on the change of volume the ratio of the volumes after and before loading is therefore approximately \(\det\mat F\).
  2. By item 2 of the same lemma \(\det\mat F\) differs from \(1 + H_{\mathrm{xx}} + H_{\mathrm{yy}} + H_{\mathrm{zz}}\) by at most \(6g^2 + 6g^3\), where \(H_{\mathrm{ij}}\) are the entries of the displacement gradient \(\mat H = \mat F - \mat I\), the partial derivatives of the displacements at \(P\), and \(g\) is the largest of their absolute values. By the assumption \(g\) is small, so this difference is small compared with \(g\).
  3. By (1.51) \(H_{\mathrm{xx}} = \varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}}\), \(H_{\mathrm{yy}} = \varepsilon_{\mathrm{yy}}\) and \(H_{\mathrm{zz}} = \varepsilon_{\mathrm{zz}}\), so the ratio of the volumes is approximately \(1 + \varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}} + \varepsilon_{\mathrm{yy}} + \varepsilon_{\mathrm{zz}} = 1 + \varepsilon_{\mathrm{v}}\).
  4. The relative change of volume is this ratio minus \(1\), so approximately \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{v}}\).

Source: SADD, PDF p. 49, BOWER §2.1.9 (PDF pp. 51-52), where \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{kk}} \approx J - 1\). The proof is not from the sources.

So the spherical part stretches or shrinks the piece equally in all directions, so that it stays similar to itself: a cube stays a cube, only larger or smaller. The deviatoric part has zero volumetric strain, so by item 3 of the lemma, applied to it, it does not change the volume to first order, but it changes the shape. SADD says this too: the spherical strain represents only the change of volume, the deviatoric strain the changes of shape (SADD, PDF p. 49).

Two examples from chapter 1. The steel cube with edge 10 mm of section 1.6.2 is glued to a table with its bottom face, and its top face is pushed by 10 µm in the direction \(x\). Its displacement field is \(u_{\mathrm{x}} = 0{,}001\,z\) and \(u_{\mathrm{y}} = u_{\mathrm{z}} = 0\). The only nonzero strain components are \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xz}} = \varepsilon_{\mathrm{zx}} = \tfrac12\,(\partial u_{\mathrm{x}}/\partial z + \partial u_{\mathrm{z}}/\partial x) = \tfrac12\,(0{,}001 + 0) = 5 \cdot 10^{-4}\), and the diagonal components are zero, since \(u_{\mathrm{x}}\) does not depend on \(x\) and \(u_{\mathrm{y}}\) and \(u_{\mathrm{z}}\) are zero. So \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{v}} = 0\), and the strain is purely deviatoric: the cube changes its shape but not its volume. For this cube we found this in section 1.6.2 with the area of a parallelogram, and now it follows from the numbers.

The steel hanging bar of length 10 m of section 1.7.1 stretches under its own weight. Only the centre \(O\) of its top end is fixed, and the weight is carried by a force spread evenly over the top face, which is the idealization of that section. The axis \(x\) points vertically down from \(O\). At the point \(P = (5\ \text{m}, 4\ \text{mm}, 0)\) the bar has the strain along the bar \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}} = 2a\,(L - x) = 2 \cdot 1{,}952 \cdot 10^{-7}\ \text{m}^{-1} \cdot 5\ \text{m} = 1{,}952 \cdot 10^{-6}\), where \(a = 1{,}952 \cdot 10^{-7}\) m⁻¹ is the constant of section 1.2 and \(L - x = 10\ \text{m} - 5\ \text{m}\), and the transverse strains \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{yy}} = \varepsilon_{\mathrm{zz}} = -0{,}3\,\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}} = -5{,}856 \cdot 10^{-7}\), where \(0{,}3\) is the ratio of thinning to stretching of steel from section 1.6. The shear components are zero. The volumetric strain is

\[\varepsilon_{\mathrm{v}} = \varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}}\,(1 - 2 \cdot 0{,}3) = 0{,}4\,\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}} = 7{,}808 \cdot 10^{-7} .\]

The factor \(0{,}4\) is \(1\) for the stretch along the bar, reduced by twice \(0{,}3\) for the thinning in the two transverse directions. So a small piece of material around \(P\) grows by \(0{,}78\) millionths of its volume, because the bar lengthens more than it thins. The spherical part stretches every fibre by \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{v}}/3 = 2{,}603 \cdot 10^{-7}\). The deviatoric strain has the components

\[\begin{aligned} e_{\mathrm{xx}} &= 1{,}952 \cdot 10^{-6} - 2{,}603 \cdot 10^{-7} = 1{,}692 \cdot 10^{-6} , \\ e_{\mathrm{yy}} = e_{\mathrm{zz}} &= -5{,}856 \cdot 10^{-7} - 2{,}603 \cdot 10^{-7} = -8{,}459 \cdot 10^{-7} , \end{aligned}\]

with the sum \(1{,}692 \cdot 10^{-6} - 2 \cdot 8{,}459 \cdot 10^{-7} = 0\) (rounded in the last digit). The piece lengthens along the bar and thins across it by half as much, so that its volume stays the same. Figure 2.86 shows both parts of the split together.

We have split stress and strain in the same way, into a part that is the same in all directions and a deviatoric part. Whether the parts are related, the mean stress to the volumetric strain and the stress deviator to the deviatoric strain, depends on the material. For a material that behaves the same in all directions we will see it in chapter 3.

All the stresses of this chapter are forces per unit area of faces in the loaded body (definition 2.20). For steel the strains are below a thousandth, so the area of a face hardly changes under loading, and it does not matter whether we measure it before or after loading. The rubber band of section 1.1, however, we stretched from 10 cm to 15 cm, and its cross section becomes noticeably smaller. To which area the stress should refer when deformations are large is the question of the next section.

2.13 Stress referred to the original shape

When we defined the stress in a bar in section 2.2, we divided the axial force by the area of the cross section before loading. We also wrote that for steel it does not matter which area we take, but for rubber it does. The traction vector of section 2.5, however, is the force per unit area of a cut in the body as it is under load. The area we divide by there is therefore the area after loading. For steel the two areas differ by less than a tenth of a per cent, so we have not noticed the difference so far. For the rubber band that we stretch from 10 cm to 15 cm (section 1.1), however, they differ by a third. Then we must say which area the force is referred to.

The equations of equilibrium at every interior point of a body were derived by Gabrio Piola in 1833 in his memoir La Meccanica de' corpi naturalmente estesi (TP1, PDF p. 434 and 435). He wanted to direct the attention of mathematicians to the principles of Lagrange's Mécanique analytique and, following Lagrange's example, he treated bodies that return to their original shape after unloading (TP1, PDF p. 435). In 1852 Kirchhoff published in the proceedings of the Vienna Academy of Sciences a memoir on the equilibrium of such a body under displacements that are not infinitely small, relying on the way indicated by Saint-Venant (TP2B, PDF p. 60). As variables he took the coordinates of the point after the displacement, not the displacements themselves, and wrote the equations of equilibrium in the usual form (TP2B, PDF p. 60). The stresses in them, however, did not have the usual meaning, for they meant forces across faces that were parallel to the coordinate planes before loading and no longer are afterwards (TP2B, PDF p. 60). So in his words these nine stresses are no longer equal in pairs (TP2B, PDF p. 60). For we proved theorem 2.36 on the symmetry of stress by the equilibrium of a small cube with faces in the coordinate planes. Faces that were parallel to these planes before loading are no longer perpendicular to each other afterwards, and such a proof does not hold for them. The stress on faces from the initial position we shall meet in definition 2.82.

The goal of this section is to write the stress also per unit area before loading, at every point of a body and on every face, not only in a bar. The route has four steps. First we compute how the area and the normal of a small piece of a face change in a deformation. Then we divide the force that acts across such a piece after loading by its area before loading. We get two new measures of stress, which books name after Piola and Kirchhoff. Next we split the deformation gradient into a stretch and a rotation and use the split to define one more measure, named after Biot. Finally we compare all the measures on the rubber band and on the steel bar and say when the difference between them matters.

We compute in the following model. We look at a point of a body that is in equilibrium after loading. At this point we know the deformation gradient \(\mat F = \mat I + \mat H\) (definition 1.110), that is, the matrix that by lemma 1.111 on a short fibre after loading maps the vector of a short fibre before loading to its vector after loading, up to a remainder that is small compared with the length of the fibre. We also know the stress components \(\sigma_{\mathrm{ab}}\) at this point, computed in the body after loading. They form the stress matrix \(\ten\sigma\) (definition 2.41), whose row \(a\) is the traction vector on the face with the normal \(\vek e_{\mathrm{a}}\). By theorem 2.36 on the symmetry of stress, \(\sigma_{\mathrm{ab}} = \sigma_{\mathrm{ba}}\), so the matrix \(\ten\sigma\) is symmetric. We assume three more things.

  1. The determinant \(J = \det\mat F\) is positive, as CM also assumes (PDF p. 126). By lemma 2.55 on the change of volume, \(J\) is the ratio of the volume of a small piece after loading to its volume before. With \(J = 0\) the piece would be squashed into a surface without volume, which matter cannot do. With \(J < 0\) it would turn into its mirror image, and by corollary 2.58 on a positive Jacobian it would have to be flattened on the way during gradual loading (section 2.10.5). We will need a nonzero determinant for the inverse matrix \(\mat F^{-1}\), and a positive one for the outward normal to stay outward and for the split of the deformation gradient into a stretch and a rotation in section 2.13.4.
  2. The pieces of faces we look at are small. So we may describe a face after loading with the deformation gradient at the point, just like fibres. For a linear displacement field, as for the band and for the sheared cube below, this description is exact.
  3. The coordinate system is the same before and after loading, as everywhere in the book (CM §3.2.1, PDF p. 112). It is right-handed (definition 2.29), because we will use the vector product.

We do not assume, however, that the strains are small. Everything that follows holds also for a band stretched by half its length.

2.13.1 Two areas

Let us start with an example. The rubber band of section 1.1 is \(L_0 = 10\) cm long before loading. Its cross section is a rectangle 2 mm wide and 1 mm thick, with the area \(A_0 = 2\ \text{mm}^2\). The index 0 means that a quantity refers to the shape before loading, as with the length \(L_0\) in section 1.6.2. We lay the axis \(x\) along the band, with the origin at its centre, the axis \(y\) along the width and the axis \(z\) along the thickness. We pull the band at both ends along the axis \(x\) until it is 15 cm long. The stretch (razmerje dolžin) of section 1.1, the new length divided by the old one, is then

\[\lambda = \frac{15\ \text{cm}}{10\ \text{cm}} = 1{,}5 .\]
